system.name: Melange influence engine (persuasion, money and cascade physics)
system.description: Behavioural simulation layer that sits downstream of the rank. It covers the shared cascade kernel and partisan edge factors, competitive independent cascade with common random numbers, contingent seeding, the flip/winnability model, money-to-lean response and defection, linear-threshold priming, salience shocks, the receptivity (susceptibility) layer, the competitiveness multiplier, electoral plays and the scenario runner. Core code: fec/moneyball_core.py and fec/engine/*.py.

components.name: Cascade activation kernel build_P and partisan edge factors
components.computes: p(u->v) = x/(x+6) with x = w x cpf x edge_mult(v). cpf_diffusion = 1 for same party and 0.4 + 0.6 sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v) across D/R. cpf_pressure = 1.7 co-partisan, 0.5 out-partisan.
components.method: One shared kernel for cascade, coalition, frontier, scenario, priming and route engines. bpf is the bipartisan share (default 0.24). The two physics factors are deliberately never merged.
assumptions: Cross-party contagion flows through bridge-builders
Co-partisan sources persuade more and out-partisan sources less (Furnas/Bakker source alignment)
Saturation constant 6 is a design choice, not estimated
Receiver susceptibility, not sender loudness, governs activation
empirical_questions: Is cross-party cosponsorship diffusion higher between high-bipartisanship pairs as sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v) predicts?
Can the saturation constant be estimated from observed cosponsorship join timing on a member's network?
Is the co-partisan / out-partisan persuasion ratio near 1.7/0.5 = 3.4 in experimental cue studies?
components.heading: Cascade activation kernel build_P and partisan edge factors

components.name: Competitive independent cascade with common random numbers
components.computes: Expected pro-CU activations in a two-colour first-to-reach race; bystanders turn anti with probability min(0.9, industry$/400000).
components.method: Keyed splitmix64 draws per (iteration, edge), reseeded with 1000003*SEED+it. SEED 7, MC 20 (scenario 40). Seed activation uses a separate 2^62 key range.
assumptions: Independent edge activations given the draws (Bharathi-Kempe-Salek competitive IC)
Industry money mobilizes neutral bystanders
MC = 20 is adequate
empirical_questions: Does the competitive IC model reproduce observed cosponsorship accumulation curves on CU bills?
Does bystander mobilization scale with industry money as min(0.9, $/400k)?
components.heading: Competitive independent cascade with common random numbers

components.name: Contingent seed activation gate
components.computes: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob(n) x SGATE[tier]); committed allies are never gated.
components.method: SGATE ranges from Highly Persuadable 1.00 down to Opponent 0.35, with unknown 0.85. seed_prob comes from the receptivity layer.
assumptions: A lobbied legislator acts only with a stance-graded take-up probability (Chen et al. UAI 2021 contingency-aware seeding)
empirical_questions: Does lobbying contact convert to cosponsorship at rates that decline with prior stance as SGATE assumes?
components.heading: Contingent seed activation gate

components.name: Flip / winnability model
components.computes: pflip = a/(a+b), where a = WM pm (c cu+1)/((c cu+1)+HALFF R) + WP nA/mAt and b is the same with industry money and anti neighbours. flip_value = sum tgt x pflip, with tgt = engagement x PERS x (1+0.3 bpf) x delivery_mult.
components.method: Saturating money term on receipts R (floored at $200k; zero imputed to median). nA = pro-neighbour weight x cpf_pressure. WM 0.35, WP 0.65, HALFF 0.10. A comment cites a Volden-Wiseman passage bonus but the code line has none.
assumptions: Money buys access more than votes (Ansolabehere; Hall & Wayman; Kalla & Broockman)
Peer proximity outweighs money
Money saturates relative to receipts
Flip-side competitive LT has no submodularity guarantee (Borodin et al.)
empirical_questions: Does relative CU vs industry money (as a share of receipts) predict roll-call alignment on CU bills after controlling for party and peers?
What is the empirical peer-vs-money weight ratio in cosponsorship decisions?
Is the effect of contributions concave in the contribution-to-receipts ratio?
components.heading: Flip - winnability model

components.name: Persuadability table PERS
components.computes: Topic target multiplier by stance tier: Champion 0.10 ... Highly Persuadable 0.65 ... Opponent 0.08; no position PERS_NONE 0.45.
components.method: Fixed design table. PERS_NONE was ratified 2026-07-02 at Ally parity. The no-position default drives about 60% of cells (open M5).
assumptions: Persuadability is inverted-U along the stance ladder
Silence equals uncertainty, not enthusiasm
empirical_questions: Is observed stance change after lobbying highest for middle tiers, as the inverted-U table assumes?
components.heading: Persuadability table PERS

components.name: Money response (lean shift) and money-triggered defection
components.computes: shift = MAXSHIFT x (r/(r+HALF)) x pressure_mult, with r = c x amount/receipts; competitor money is multiplied by LOSSFRAME 1.10. Defection moves floor(|shift|/DTHRESH) rungs; Champion and Opponent are immune.
components.method: MAXSHIFT 18 (cut from 40), HALF 0.10, DTHRESH 11.25. Crossing one rung takes roughly a sixth of receipts.
assumptions: Money moves positions little (null vote-buying literature)
Threats weigh more than gifts (loss aversion, elite-attenuated)
empirical_questions: Do large competitor spends precede measurable stance shifts in press or votes?
Is the effective loss/gain asymmetry for legislators near 1.10?
components.heading: Money response (lean shift) and money-triggered defection

components.name: Linear-threshold priming (cheapest tip)
components.computes: For each target, the cheapest mix of recruiting pro neighbours and money that closes theta - pressure.
components.method: theta = tier threshold (0.6 ... 3.0) + max(0, -lean/120) + 0.25 per Opponent cell. Cross-party cue factor sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v) (Bakker-Lelkes-Malka). Recruit cost = CEDGE x 0.5 / PERS[tier]. Money closes the gap only up to 0.97 pm units.
assumptions: Linear-threshold adoption over summed neighbour pressure
Out-party cues do not persuade
empirical_questions: Do members join CU bills after a threshold share of their close cosponsorship partners has joined?
Are out-party cosponsors' endorsements ineffective at recruiting new cosponsors?
components.heading: Linear-threshold priming (cheapest tip)

components.name: Salience shock (Noble-Turner going public)
components.computes: Rally, retreat and backfire probabilities per issue, member steps, and a go-public advisory.
components.method: z = min(1, |D-R tier gap|/3); psi = uncertainty; b = min(0.35, 0.05 + 0.10 psi); p = (1-b)(1-z), q = (1-b)z. Rally: co-partisan +1, out-partisan +0.5 if bpf >= 0.30. Retreat: co +1, out -1. Vulnerable members x1.35 x susc_mult. Defensive appeal raises the threshold by (1 + DELTA/2).
assumptions: Co-partisans move more than out-partisans under salience (Noble & Turner 2024)
Backfire grows with policy uncertainty
Electorally vulnerable members respond more
empirical_questions: After a public campaign on a CU issue, do co-partisans of the campaign's champions shift more than out-partisans?
Does polarization of an issue predict whether going public polarizes positions further (retreat regime)?
components.heading: Salience shock (Noble-Turner going public)

components.name: Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)
components.computes: Per member: susc, susc_mult [0.70, 1.30], edge_mult [0.80, 1.20], pressure_mult = clip(susc x incent x pt, 0.50, 1.60), and seed_prob = clip(0.60 + 0.10 coop + 0.06 breadth + 0.04 visibility, 0.30, 0.90). The rank is not affected.
components.method: Behavioural basis (default): susc = .40 cooperation_v2 + .30 N(affective) - .20 diligence - .10 dominance, blended 0.70/0.30 with persona when n >= 15 cues. Lexical basis: .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E. incent: retiring 0.60, else clip(1 + .30(comp - 0.5), 0.85, 1.15), neutral when COMPET_MULT is on. pt: 1.15 loss domain, 0.92 safe. PERSONA_W 0.30 is kept by owner ruling. Recorded double-count: cooperation_v2 vs bpf rho +0.888.
assumptions: Neuroticism degrades decisions under pressure (Byrne et al. 2015); the A, C and E signs are design priors, not Byrne findings
Final-term members are less responsive (Fouirnaies & Hall)
Members in a live race are in the loss domain and take risks (Linde & Vis 2016)
No N susceptibility signal has been demonstrated (Nokken-Poole drift MISS; H5 null)
empirical_questions: Do higher-susceptibility members change cosponsorship or votes more after lobbying contact (prospective H2)?
Are retiring members less responsive to PAC money in roll-call alignment?
Do members in competitive races take riskier positions on CU issues than safe-seat members?
components.heading: Receptivity layer (susceptibility, incentive, prospect domain, seed probability)

components.name: Competitiveness multiplier c (COMPET_MULT)
components.computes: c = 1 + 1.0 x exp(-max(lean, 0)/5.0), range (1, 2], where lean = Cook PVI oriented to the member's party. It scales effective dollars on both money legs.
components.method: Matched by Cook incumbent or district, with overrides; unmatched members get 1.0. Default ON since 2026-10-06 (D-104/D-105/D-107/D-108). Real dollars are unchanged.
assumptions: Dollars buy more in competitive seats (reciprocity NOT validated)
AMPLITUDE and SCALE are uncalibrated owner judgment
empirical_questions: Is the marginal effect of PAC contributions on access or alignment larger in competitive seats?
What decay scale in PVI points best fits contribution-effect heterogeneity?
brain_notes: C:/Users/pgoff/Documents/brain/topics/2026-10-05 competitiveness lane (brain ledger D-104, D-105, D-107, D-108)
components.heading: Competitiveness multiplier c (COMPET_MULT)

components.name: Electoral security, leverage and contest/defend plays
components.computes: Security percentile from Ballotpedia Election_Average; leverage = 1 + 0.8(1 - security); play routes contest-primary, contest-general, defend or none.
components.method: Defend value = comp x positive gap vs the cross-party average. Contest route = the larger of the primary and general gaps. Contest plays convert opponents in spread().
assumptions: Ballotpedia electoral average measures security
empirical_questions: Are CU PAC dollars more effective (in later alignment) in members with lower electoral security?
components.heading: Electoral security, leverage and contest-defend plays

components.name: Scenario runner (what-if)
components.computes: Change in coalition spread and flip value under user money, defection or stance moves, using CRN at MC 40.
components.method: A defection shifts all movable positions by at most 1 fine tier.
assumptions: A defection is a general disposition shift across issues
empirical_questions: When members switch stance on one CU issue, do they shift on other CU issues too?
components.heading: Scenario runner (what-if)

components.name: Priority anchor, leave-one-out orientation and engagement signal
components.computes: Topic priority = tier anchor (1, 2/3, 1/3, 0) + alpha x IMP-weighted stance on other topics (alpha 0.15 flip / 0.25 coalition); engagement = block-weighted legislative activity; base = max(0, eng + 0.15 x priority).
components.method: Leave-one-topic-out orientation. Fails closed on an incomplete roster.
assumptions: Stance on other CU issues predicts priority on this issue
empirical_questions: Does leave-one-topic-out stance predict stance on the held-out topic?
components.heading: Priority anchor, leave-one-out orientation and engagement signal

positions.paul_position: Paul treats influence probabilities on directed edges as foundational (Fink), and reads source identity and party as filters on receptiveness (Furnas). The cpf_pressure split encodes this. The saturation constant has no literature basis.

citations: Kim J. et al. 2025 (conflicting industries margin note)
Fink et al. 2023 (Viral Centrality vs Monte Carlo)
positions.paul_position: Paul wants rival industries modeled, and Monte Carlo-style scenario simulation that is cheap to compute (Viral Centrality). The system chose Monte Carlo with common random numbers instead.
Paul maps contingency-aware seeding directly to legislators who may or may not move when approached, and to probabilistic lobbying commitment. This is implemented as SGATE.

Paul believes money buys access and returns, but he also highlighted that lobbying sways undecided members more than donations (Jacoby). His Bonica margin note asks for a short-term theory of engagement and treatment of sunk costs. The model's 'money buys access not votes' stance agrees with his sources but is more conservative than his ROI enthusiasm.
Paul reads ideologically fluid, competitive seats (his example is Fitzpatrick) and centrists as the most movable. This is consistent with the inverted-U, but he never tested it.
Highlights support the reflection effect and loss framing in MPs, weaker than in the public. Paul's notes do not discuss defection mechanics.

citations: Chen 2023 margin note on high-ranking members
positions.paul_position: Paul hypothesizes that coalition formation is a complex contagion. His margin note says pressure from high-ranking members is 'not diminishing', which challenges submodular assumptions.
Paul highlighted Noble & Turner heavily (rally, retreat, backfire, defensive appeals) but did not annotate it. The component implements that model almost directly.

Paul wants psychological traits to adjust the response to pressure, placed as edge parameters (Oropeza). He notes that 10 personalities collapse into 4 observable ones. The system's validity record undercuts this more than his notes acknowledge.
Paul endorses Cook PVI as a vulnerability measure and reads competitive seats as responsive. No source he annotated says dollars buy more in competitive seats.
Paul highlighted Bonica's finding that donors direct funds to competitive races under the partisan electoral model. There is no annotation.
Monte Carlo is treated as a tool. Paul highlighted Weimer's use of Monte Carlo as a negative control.

evidence.title: 2024 House At-A-Glance
evidence.claim: Cook's table separates PVI from race rating. Parsed per district row (435 rows), the 24 Toss Ups span R+8 (AK-AL) to D+5 (CA-22, NY-04). The six EVEN seats get five different ratings: FL-27 Solid R, PA-01 Likely R, NH-01 Likely D, PA-17 Lean D, CO-08 and NE-02 Toss Up. Seats at D+2 or D+3 are Solid D (AZ-04, CT-02, GA-02), Lean D (CT-05, NY-03) or Toss Up (OR-05, CA-45, NY-17; all three held by Republicans). Window: 2024 cycle as of 2024-09-12. Denominator: 435 districts.
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5), lean = Cook PVI oriented to the member's party (Cook 2026 district PVI for House). Any seat at EVEN or leaning against the member gets the maximum c = 2.0. Illustration with this table's 2024 PVIs: Salazar (EVEN, Solid R) and Bacon (EVEN, Toss Up) both get 2.0; Stanton (D, D+2, Solid D) gets about 1.67, whereas the table's D+2 Toss Up incumbents (Chavez-DeRemer OR-05, Steel CA-45) are Republicans, so lean = -2 and c = 2.0; Courtney (D+3, Solid D) and Suozzi (D+3, Lean D) both get about 1.55. Verifier arithmetic on 2024 PVIs, not the live 2026 artifact.
evidence.transfer: The structural point carries over: PVI is a partisan baseline, while the rating adds incumbent and candidate factors. The numbers do not carry over: they use 2024 PVIs, which come from the 2016 and 2020 presidential results, and 2024 ratings, while the system reads Cook 2026 PVIs for the 119th Congress roster. It applies only to House members; senators use Paul's state PVI table. The table says nothing about whether money works better in competitive seats, so it neither validates nor refutes the reciprocity premise behind c.

evidence.title: 2024 House At-A-Glance
evidence.claim: Cook's rating differs from PVI for incumbents with personal electoral strength. Fitzpatrick is EVEN and Likely R. Salazar is EVEN and Solid R. Cuellar is D+3 and Likely D, while Hayes is D+3 and Lean D. A candidate-specific vulnerability signal therefore carries information that PVI lacks.
evidence.system_side: The Fouirnaies-Hall incentive term 1+.30*(comp-0.5) takes comp = 1 - security from Ballotpedia vote results, so it is candidate-specific. With COMPET_MULT on (the default), this term is set to neutral (1.0) and the PVI-only c carries competitiveness instead. As a result, the engine path no longer sees candidate-specific vulnerability.
evidence.transfer: This is the clearest example of the PVI-versus-rating gap affecting a live dial. It holds as long as COMPET_MULT=1 neutralizes the Ballotpedia comp term. A 2024 snapshot cannot calibrate 119th-Congress values; it only shows that the two measures diverge.

evidence.title: 2024 House At-A-Glance
evidence.claim: The table gives a forward-looking expert risk category (Solid, Likely, Lean, Toss Up) for each seat, along with OPEN and VACANT flags: 41 OPEN lines and 4 VACANT seats as of 2024-09-12.
evidence.system_side: build_electoral.py (writes electoral.json, not electoral_plays.json): security is a percentile of Ballotpedia's backward-looking Election_Average; leverage = 1 + LELEV*(1 - security), LELEV default 0.8; unmatched members get neutral security 0.5.
evidence.transfer: Useful only as the design pattern for a dated, forward-looking risk input. Using it would require the current-cycle Cook ratings, dated before the decision, not this 2024 table. Open-seat retirees would also need the same retiring treatment the receptivity layer already gives them.

evidence.title: A causal approach for detecting team-level momentum in NBA games
evidence.claim: The paper's Monte Carlo is a negative control for an estimator applied to observed data: simulate data with no effect, re-run the matching estimator, expect a null.
evidence.system_side: scenario.py uses Monte Carlo as a forward model: baseline vs scenario competitive-cascade spread under edge-keyed common random numbers (SEED=7, MC default 40), so an unperturbed scenario gives a zero delta by construction. That is an identity property of the simulator, not a negative control on an inferred effect.
evidence.transfer: A Weimer-style placebo applies to empirical estimators that read observed outcomes (forecasters, the contract), not to the forward cascade's deltas, which are model outputs.

evidence.title: Should Moving to the Middle Win Candidates Votes? It Depends Where Voters Are
evidence.claim: Moving on an issue is rewarded only where the audience disagrees with the current position, and it is penalized where the audience holds that position (Republican candidate, own=R -0.0364 vs own=D +0.0404, Table A8).
evidence.system_side: PERS is a fixed multiplier keyed to a member's stance tier: Champion 0.10, Highly Persuadable 0.65, Persuadable 0.60, Opponent 0.08, and PERS_NONE 0.45 for silence. Callers such as flip_model.py and per_topic_flip.py apply it per topic/scenario stance cell, so persuadability is already issue-specific, which matches the paper's issue-level logic.
evidence.transfer: This is an analogy only. The paper studies voters choosing between candidates, not legislators being lobbied. It gives no evidence on legislator persuadability or on the shape of the PERS curve, and it should not be read as calibrating PERS values. Its one structural point, that the target of an appeal is the issue-level disagreement and not the aggregate midpoint, is consistent with PERS being applied per topic.

evidence.title: Introduction To Monte Carlo Simulation
evidence.claim: Many simulations follow three steps: model the system as PDFs, sample from them repeatedly, and tally the statistics of interest. Drawbacks: simulation can need huge computing resources, gives no exact solutions, is only as good as the model and inputs, and its software is prone to bugs. Analytic and experimental alternatives should be considered before committing to simulation.
evidence.system_side: The cascade fits the three-step pattern. Each edge is a Bernoulli draw with p = x/(x+6), x = w * cpf_diffusion(u,v) * edge_mult(v), from build_P. An edge fires when the splitmix64 draw keyed by (iteration, edge) is below p. Each run counts A-coloured nodes (seeds included) and the spread is tot/MC over iterations (MC = 20 default in budget_frontier.py, 40 in scenario.py). Unestimated inputs: the saturation constant 6, the bystander rule min(0.9, $/400k), and the 0.4 + 0.6 sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v) cross-party factor.
evidence.transfer: The recipe and caveats are generic, so they carry over fully. They say nothing about whether the cascade parameters are right, which IC model to use, or whether MC = 20 is enough. The paper does not cover common random numbers or variance reduction. Read it as a warning about inputs, not as support for the design.

evidence.title: Introduction To Monte Carlo Simulation
evidence.claim: Monte Carlo is a key tool for analytically intractable problems. Some feel it is overused as a lazy way out, and analytic and experimental alternatives should be considered before committing to simulation.
evidence.system_side: The scenario runner reruns the competitive cascade at MC = 40 under edge-keyed CRN for money, defection and stance moves. The sibling flip channel is closed-form: flip_model.pflip returns a/(a+b). The in-browser desk computes break-even/marginal effects as tgt * (pflip_new - pfbase) from the same closed form. Simulation is used for the cascade spread.
evidence.transfer: The split between closed-form flip math and MC spread fits the paper's advice. The paper offers nothing on which analytic proxy (Viral Centrality, Katz-Bonacich) might replace the cascade MC; that comparison would need its own test.

evidence.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
evidence.claim: Going public is more attractive when the status quo is favorable: c(-1) > c(1) always (Prop 2). Under Partisan Retreat the president never goes public against an unfavorable status quo (c_q(1) < 0) but always has an incentive to defend a favorable one. The model predicts that going public occurs more often in defense of a favorable status quo than to win policy change (p.25). The defensive appeal logic depends on the co-partisan being the relevant pivot, which holds only when the status quo is favorable (p.15, p.22-23).
evidence.system_side: defensive_appeal_value() runs for every issue with no status-quo check. The advisory value is E_dspread + 1.5 x len(defections_prevented) for offense and defend issues alike. In the live salience_advisory.json (2026-10-08 15:37, 18 issues), the four GO PUBLIC verdicts (top quartile, cut 68.27) are all sq=offense, and each is driven by held counts: Technology & Emerging (E_dspread -3.87, held 67, q=0.83), Member Business Lending (+5.83, held 60), Data Privacy (-19.35, held 68) and Fraud Prevention (-9.73, held 52). The three defend issues rank 13th to 15th. Tech & Emerging is close to the paper's pure-retreat case on an unfavorable status quo, where the paper says never go public, yet it is ranked first. The dashboard bundle surfaces these verdicts as 'GO PUBLIC · holds N'. The figures were reproduced by the verifier from the same 2026-10-08 file and code. They are heuristic advisory scores over 18 issues, not measured effects.
evidence.transfer: No empirical transfer is needed. This is an internal-consistency check against the model the code claims to implement. The contradiction holds whenever the defensive credit is added on sq='offense' issues. Gating held to sq=='defend' would restore the paper's ordering. Whether the paper's ordering is right for a CU advocacy campaign is a separate, untested question.

evidence.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
evidence.claim: Sincere legislative polarization z and base-pressure reactions (beta_L, beta_R, with probabilities p, q, 1-p-q) are separate primitives that the authors vary independently. The infrastructure illustration (Pew 2019 partisan gap of 7 points vs 46 on health care) is presented as a case where elite polarization exceeds mass polarization and a Rally is still possible.
evidence.system_side: salience_issue_params estimates z as the absolute D-R gap in mean legislator stance tier. It then sets q = (1-b) x min(1, z/3) and p = (1-b)(1 - z/3). The elite stance gap therefore sets the mass-base reaction odds. The resulting regime mixture drives both the advisory and the dashboard exec cue.
evidence.transfer: The mapping is a design choice, not something the paper implies. It holds only if base reactions on CU issues track legislator stance gaps. That would need a base-side or mass-opinion measure, such as a partisan gap in public or credit-union-member opinion per issue, which the system does not have. The paper's own example warns that the two can diverge.

evidence.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
evidence.claim: psi bounds a common preference shock and stands for informational policy uncertainty. Higher psi makes the president weakly less likely to go public and shrinks the favorable-vs-unfavorable gap (Prop 5). The paper never links psi to the probability of Backfire. Under a favorable status quo, going public can pay even when backfire is certain (the threshold on beta_L falls as z and delta rise).
evidence.system_side: psi = 1 - (share of members with a stance tier) + 0.3 x (True-Neutral share). This measures missing posture data, not uncertainty about preferences. Backfire is b = min(0.35, 0.05 + 0.10 psi), labelled 'Prop 5 caution'. The actual Prop 5 effect (damping go-public value) sits behind SAL_PSI_DAMP, which defaults to 0, so it appears only as a text tag at psi >= 0.8. Backfire steps are always non-positive, so the favorable-status-quo case where backfire still pays is not represented.
evidence.transfer: Data missingness stands in for psi only if a member's lack of a stance label reflects real preference uncertainty rather than collection gaps. Coverage is known to differ by party and chamber (press collector). The b-psi link has no support in this paper and should be cited as a design prior.

evidence.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
evidence.claim: Section 4 lets the president's silent-reelection probability rho(x_sq) vary. A higher rho lowers the go-public range. When rho(-1) > rho(1) and psi > psi*, the president may 'gamble for reelection' by going public on an unfavorable status quo (Prop 6, Eq. 15). Legislators' delta is their stake in their party winning the White House, not in their own seats. Caveat: Prop 6's first bullet (p.44) states the opposite direction for an electorally weak President, so the paper is internally inconsistent on the rho direction.
evidence.system_side: VULN multiplies every legislator's salience step by 1.35 if the member has a defend or contest electoral play, with the comment 'Noble A.4: gambling for reelection'. In backfire, co-partisans with a live race are held at 0 ('delta dominates base: Sec 3.1').
evidence.transfer: This paper does not support the amplifier. Its rho and the gambling logic concern the actor who goes public (the president), not the responsiveness of rank-and-file legislators. Any support for 'electorally vulnerable members respond more' has to come from elsewhere (for example, the electoral-incentives literature), and the 1.35 constant is uncalibrated.

evidence.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
evidence.claim: There are three base-reaction regimes: Rally (both toward), Partisan Retreat (co toward, out away) and Backfire (both away, out more). The single restriction is beta_L > beta_R: co-partisans always favor the president's proposal more than out-partisans do. Going public adds the electoral stake delta to the thresholds as z + beta_L + delta/2 and -z + beta_R - delta/2 (Eqs. 1-2).
evidence.system_side: steps_for() sets the base co-partisan step above the out-partisan step in all three regimes. Per-member VULN and susc_mult multipliers apply before rounding, so the ordering can fail for individual members. Rally is co +1, out +0.5 only if bpf >= 0.30. Retreat is co +1, out -1. Backfire is co 0 or -0.5, out -1. The dashboard exec cue (EXECP='R') applies the same p, q, b mixture to bystander mobilization. The defensive channel instead scales the money-defection threshold multiplicatively, by DTHRESH x (1 + DELTA/2) with DELTA = 0.5. The actor is generalized from the president to a CU-side campaign whose party is set by --party.
evidence.transfer: The regime structure transfers most cleanly to the dashboard's executive cue, which matches the paper's presidential actor in a federal two-party Congress. It transfers less well to an ACU or industry 'going public' actor, which has no reelection tied to the outcome. The delta channel exists only because co-partisans share the president's electoral fate. The bpf >= 0.30 cutoff, the step sizes and the multiplicative delta are the code's own design, not the paper's. The paper's delta is additive in the vote threshold and has no money-defection analog.

evidence.title: Presidential Leadership and Legislative Polarization
evidence.claim: 'Gridlock region' means the range of the common preference shock theta over which two pivots keep the status quo. Going public always widens it, even under a Rally, because asymmetric base pressure creates 'effective polarization'.
evidence.system_side: gridlock_width counts members whose tier sits in a five-rung MIDBAND, and E_dmidband reports its change. The comments read a falling count as 'Prop 1 hollowing' and a rising count on defend issues as a win. The count is reported but not used in the verdict.
evidence.transfer: Occupancy of a middle band among 533 members is a different quantity from a shock interval between two pivots. Prop 1 makes no prediction about its sign, so the metric cannot be read as testing or reproducing Prop 1.

evidence.title: Do Politicians Take Risks Like the Rest of Us? An Experimental Test of Prospect Theory Under MPs
evidence.claim: Loss aversion was NOT found in the MP sample (n=46) nor in the student sample; the authors suspect the loss-aversion tasks lack validity (participants may treat the endowment as house money, fn 4). The abstract's claim that MPs' deviations are 'somewhat smaller than those of other people' is not a formal statistical test in the main text: it rests on the authors' student comparison sample (n=176, Appendix E, not in the file; e.g. students showed the common ratio effect, MPs did not, p.106) plus prior literature.
evidence.system_side: shift_lean multiplies competitor-source money by LOSSFRAME 1.10 so a competitor 'threat' moves lean more than an equal CU gift. The code comment cites K&T loss aversion 'elite-attenuated per Linde-Vis', and audit_full locks this asymmetry in as by design. Defection then moves floor(|shift|/DTHRESH) rungs.
evidence.transfer: The paper is no basis for LOSSFRAME. (1) It reports no loss aversion in politicians, so the citation runs against the dial. (2) Its loss frame concerns outcomes for the decision-maker relative to a reference point; a competitor PAC donation to a member is not a loss to that member, so the 'threat frame' is a separate untested assumption. (3) 1.10 is not derived from any number in the paper. LOSSFRAME stands as owner judgment and should be cited as such.

evidence.title: Do Politicians Take Risks Like the Rest of Us? An Experimental Test of Prospect Theory Under MPs
evidence.claim: Strong reflection effect in the paid lottery task: risky choice 39.13% under gain vs 76.09% under loss (36.96 pp, binomial p=0.0002, n=46). In the four hypothetical scenarios (Table 4, Fisher tests): economic 45% vs 50% (p=0.774), votes 45.83% vs 40.91% (p=0.774), votes+economic 85% vs 69.23% (p=0.302), Asian disease 88.46% vs 30% (p<0.001). In a logistic regression over all four scenarios (n=164, covariates, clustered SEs) the scenario-specific loss-frame odds ratios are 0.860 (economic, p=0.827), 1.599 (votes, p=0.490), 8.684 (votes+economic, p=0.033) and 14.633 (Asian disease, p=0.001). Reflection thus appears in two of four scenarios; votes look like the reference point ('less strong but nevertheless suggestive'). Time in parliament does not predict risk-taking (OR 0.995, p=0.580).
evidence.system_side: pt_domain = loss if the member has a defend or contest electoral play, or security < 0.45. pt_mult = 1.15 for loss ('gambles under threat, more movable') and 0.92 for gain. It enters pressure_mult = clip(susc_mult x incent x pt, 0.50, 1.60) (pressure_mult_compet when COMPET_MULT is on), which scales the money terms in shift_lean and in pflip. The docstring also says politicians are 'loss-averse overall'.
evidence.transfer: Carries over: the reflection effect is real in politicians, and votes are the more plausible reference dimension, which fits keying the domain on a live race. Does not: (a) framing was randomly assigned in hypothetical scenarios, not inferred from seat security; (b) the sample is 46 Dutch MPs, 2014-2015, 76.2% right-wing; mapping onto US seat security is untested; (c) risk-seeking here means preferring higher-variance options, not greater responsiveness to money or pressure; (d) the 1.15/0.92 magnitudes and 'loss-averse overall' are unsupported (no loss aversion found). The votes+economic OR 8.684 is a scenario-specific interaction in a regression that pools scenarios; quote it with that label and alongside the non-significant Fisher test (p=0.302).

evidence.title: Strategic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
evidence.claim: Lobbying links follow first-time donations immediately and decline over the next three years; the paper measures lobbying-legislative links, not votes, and cites Fowler, Garro and Spenkuch (2020) for no quid-pro-quo returns to corporate PAC donations even if donations buy access.
evidence.system_side: WM=0.35, WP=0.65 with code comment 'money is the minority partner ... money buys access/effort > votes'. CU money (congestion.json cu) and competitor money (banks+finserv) enter as static levels with Michaelis-Menten saturation on receipts (HALFF). No onset or recency term.
evidence.transfer: Consistent with the access-not-votes stance but gives no vote-shift evidence, so it cannot calibrate WM/WP or HALFF. It implies the lobbying-link value of money is onset-driven and transient, which a static cycle-level money term ignores. Sample is public manufacturing firms; the system models CU/bank money.

evidence.title: How Do Electoral Incentives Affect Legislator Behavior? Evidence from U.S. State Legislatures
evidence.claim: Removing reelection incentives lowers visible effort: the productivity index falls -0.24 SD (SE 0.03), with a range of -0.09 to -0.41 across specifications. Ideological positioning does not shift: |W-NOMINATE| +0.02 (SE 0.01), the party-split estimates are about 0, and interest-group ratings show no systematic change. The authors argue that legislators who run for other offices keep their electoral incentives, so the estimates are likely a lower bound.
evidence.system_side: incent_mult = 0.60 for every member on fec/retiring_members.txt. The docstring (receptivity_layer.py:15-16) cites Fouirnaies & Hall for final-term members reducing 'effort/responsiveness'; the retiring list header calls them 'less responsive to pressure'. The factor enters pressure_mult = clip(susc*incent*pt, 0.50, 1.60). The list header says it 'Includes members seeking OTHER office (Golden/Barr/Stefanik etc.)', and Andy Barr is the first entry. Line 129 (and docstring lines 17-19) also attribute the competitiveness term 1+.30(comp-0.5) to Fouirnaies-Hall, but the paper does not test seat competitiveness.
evidence.transfer: Weak for the 0.60 size and the 'responsiveness' reading. The paper estimates effort allocation in low-salience state chambers under exogenous, binding term limits. It does not estimate response to lobbying or money, and its null on positions points against extra movability or immovability. Congressional retirement is voluntary and self-selected, which is the confound the paper's within-person design is built to avoid. Its lower-bound argument (p.672) contradicts treating members who seek other office as having no electoral incentive. The direction (less effort in the final term) carries over; the magnitude and the mechanism of 'pressure response' do not.

evidence.title: The Effect of Political Advertising after Citizens United: Adjusting for Unmeasured Confounding in Marginal Structural Models
evidence.claim: Groups may target markets with more persuadable voters using a metric the researcher cannot see, so a naive comparison of treated and untreated units is confounded. The paper handles only time-constant unmeasured confounding, through unit fixed effects in the propensity score. Time-varying unmeasured confounding still breaks identification.
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0 x exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0) scales effective dollars on both money legs. AMPLITUDE and SCALE are Paul's judgment constants, uncalibrated, and the reciprocity they encode is explicitly NOT validated.
evidence.transfer: No direct transfer. The paper estimates effects of ads on voters, not the responsiveness of legislators to PAC dollars, and it must not be cited as support for c (D-104..D-108). Its only bearing is on calibration: any future attempt to estimate c from observed giving and alignment must handle strategic targeting of competitive seats, because givers pick those seats on information the analyst lacks.

evidence.title: D-NOMINATE After 10 Years: A Comparative Update to Congress: A Political Economic History of Roll Call Voting
evidence.claim: The linear model is not a striking improvement over the constant model, about 0.3 percent in both chambers (Table 1: House 2D constant 85.65 vs linear 5-Congress 85.96; Senate 84.04 vs 84.40). The authors let legislators serving as few as 3 Congresses get linear terms, admitting random walkers will appear linear, a bias deliberately in favour of the polynomial models.
evidence.system_side: susc_trait includes N at weight .30 (lines 186 and 189) and is blended with persona z at line 191. The brain records the Tier-1 Nokken-Poole drift gate (2026-07-08, n = 441) as MISS on all candidates and a real verdict; N stays in the blend unverified; 'NOT more looks on drift'.
evidence.transfer: Interpretation only: low true-score variance in drift is consistent with the MISS but does not overturn or reopen it. Supports the brain's listed alternative (CU-specific vote-switch criterion), not another look.

evidence.title: D-NOMINATE After 10 Years: A Comparative Update to Congress: A Political Economic History of Roll Call Voting
evidence.claim: Across Congresses 1-105, a constant ideal point per legislator classifies almost as well as a linear one (about 0.3 percent difference); linear change captured most of the relatively small changes in positions.
evidence.system_side: MAXSHIFT default 18 (cut from 40, 'money moves POSITIONS little'); DTHRESH 11.25; COMMITTED = {Champion, Opponent} are the only rungs immune to money defection.
evidence.transfer: Indirect: the paper measures general-ideology stability with no money treatment, so it supports only a low prior on position change, not any MAXSHIFT or DTHRESH value.

evidence.title: D-NOMINATE After 10 Years: A Comparative Update to Congress: A Political Economic History of Roll Call Voting
evidence.claim: The second dimension now adds less than 1 percent improvement over the first dimension in both chambers.
evidence.system_side: blended_engine_priority adds PRIORITY_ORIENTATION_ALPHA (0.15 flip, 0.25 coalition) times engine_orientation, a fixed-IMP-weighted mean of the member's category stance scores excluding the current topic.
evidence.transfer: engine_orientation reads category_stance scores, not votes. The Path V vote shares (UNVERIFIED) show opposite party direction across some categories (CFPB, Technology, Exam, CU Capital Requirements lean R; Charter, NCUA Budget & Insurance lean D) and none in others. If stance scores share that pattern, leave-one-out borrowing could import party sign; that has not been checked on the stance scores. Alpha is small.

evidence.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
evidence.claim: Kang (2016) structural Tullock-contest model of energy policy (538 policies in 445 bills, 110th Congress): lobbying raises enactment probability by only 0.021%-0.415% relative to an 8% baseline, while average returns to lobbying are estimated at 137% (renewables) to 152% (oil and gas). The review reads both as possible misspecification. The separate point that observable contributions miss other influence channels comes from the Farm Bill / Bombardini and Trebbi (2011) discussion, not from Kang.
evidence.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where money is the minority partner (WM 0.35 vs peer weight WP 0.65). The money term saturates relative to the member's receipts (HALFF 0.10), on the stated premise that money buys access and effort more than votes.
evidence.transfer: Kang measures firm lobbying expenditure against provision-level enactment in the energy sector. Melange's money leg is PAC contributions against member-level winnability on CU topics. The review supports only the direction (small marginal effect of money), not the WM/WP split or the HALFF constant, which remain unestimated design choices. The evidence is federal and from 2007-08.

evidence.title: Empirical Models of Lobbying
evidence.claim: Structural work finds a very small marginal enactment effect of lobbying (Kang 0.021%-0.415%) despite large stakes, and campaign contributions are low with federal donation caps very seldom binding (Ansolabehere et al. 2003, as reported).
evidence.system_side: MAXSHIFT was cut from 40 to 18 on the premise that money moves positions little. A defection requires a donation of about one sixth of the member's receipts, so a $10k gift shifts median receipts by about 0.9 lean, far below DTHRESH 11.25.
evidence.transfer: The review addresses enactment and bill outcomes, not shifts in individual member stance. It supports rare money-triggered defection but not the LOSSFRAME 1.10 asymmetry or the specific constants.

evidence.title: Learnable Skills, or Unteachable Instinct? What Can and What Cannot Be Taught in the Lobbying Profession
evidence.claim: Evidence on campaign finance's impact is at best mixed (Baumgartner and Leech 1998). 'Very few' lobbyists take part in campaign finance, and those who do are partisan (Koger and Victor 2009). The authors conclude that campaign money matters less to lobbying than popular belief holds. No figure is given.
evidence.system_side: pflip uses WM = 0.35 for money and WP = 0.65 for peer proximity. The code comment says money is the minority partner and buys access, not votes. Money terms saturate relative to receipts.
evidence.transfer: The paper agrees with the ordering (money below relationships and information) but gives no estimate. It relies on secondary sources from 1998-2009. It speaks about lobbyists' personal giving, not PAC money given to members, so it cannot calibrate the 0.35/0.65 split or HALFF.

evidence.title: Conflating Lobbying and PACs: The Surprisingly Low Overlap in Organizational Lobbying and Campaign Expenditures
evidence.claim: About 75% of 1998-2018 lobbying expenditures came from organizations that also gave through PACs. The top lobbying groups almost always have affiliated PACs. Organizations doing both average $403,435 a year in lobbying (IQR $118,825-$1,558,597) vs $64,000 for lobby-only organizations (IQR $30,000-$130,000). Even so, 64-70% of politically active organizations per year lobby without a PAC.
evidence.system_side: In pflip the opposing side b = WM*pm*(cm*ind+1)/((cm*ind+1)+HALFF*R) + WP*nB/mBt: an opposing-industry money leg built from ind0 = banks + finserv from congestion.json (industry PAC money), saturated against member receipts, plus a peer/network leg. WM=0.35, WP=0.65. No lobbying-spend term enters b.
evidence.transfer: PAC money should flag the biggest lobbying spenders, since the paper finds those almost always have PACs; organizations that lobby without a PAC contribute nothing to b's money leg. Whether specific finance opponents (ABA, ICBA, large banks, fintech or crypto firms) fall in either group is the analyst's assumption, not in the paper. The paper tests neither access nor votes and gives no support for the WM/WP split. UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

evidence.title: Moneyed Interests, Information, and Action in Congress: A Survey Experiment
evidence.claim: Pooled over all staff, minimal evidence that think-tank evidence raises siding with the requester (if anything, less likely than 'own analysis'). Split by party, aligned think-tank evidence raises siding and non-aligned lowers it, and for both parties the non-aligned penalty is roughly twice the aligned benefit (Fig. 4). The reference category is stated inconsistently: 'own analysis' in the p.12 prose, 'supportive polling' in the Fig. 4 note. Stated intentions; N=441 staff (5.2% response), 549 ratings per factor; party subgroup Ns not reported.
evidence.system_side: cpf_pressure multiplies co-partisan member-to-member pressure by 1.7 and out-partisan pressure by 0.5. The kernel docstring cites 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment' as the basis. Relative to 1.0, the system's gain (+0.7) is larger than its penalty (-0.5).
evidence.transfer: The paper randomises the ideology of an outside requester's evidence and records DC staffers' stated likelihood of siding with it (2017, single hypothetical). The system applies the factor to legislator-to-legislator cosponsor edges, where the partisan relation is between two Members, not an evidence source. That supports the direction of a source-alignment term, but not its 3.4 ratio or the gain-over-penalty asymmetry. If anything, the paper points to a penalty larger than the gain. The pooled estimate is null over the party fault line, so any figure taken from the paper must be quoted by party stratum or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.

evidence.title: Moneyed Interests, Information, and Action in Congress: A Survey Experiment
evidence.claim: Donors are not granted meetings more readily than geographic constituents; Democratic staff are less likely to meet donors. This is contrary to Kalla & Broockman 2016 and consistent with Chin, Bond & Geva 2000. Staff say they are much less likely to use information from donors. They are relatively more likely to side with donors than to meet them or use their information, which the authors leave unresolved. The authors also find no preferential access for donors qua donors.
evidence.system_side: WM 0.35 vs WP 0.65 makes money the minority partner, justified by 'money buys access/effort > votes (Ansolabehere; Hall & Wayman; Kalla & Broockman)'. Peer proximity nA/nB uses party-only cpf_pressure.
evidence.transfer: The evidence agrees that money is a minor lever on positions. It contradicts the access half of the code comment, at least for stated staff intentions in 2017: a request framed as coming from a donor gets no meeting premium. The vignette varies requester identity, not dollar amounts, so it says nothing about the shape of the saturating money term or about HALFF. Social desirability may push stated donor meetings down, as the authors warn, and that limits how far the evidence carries.

evidence.title: Moneyed Interests, Information, and Action in Congress: A Survey Experiment
evidence.claim: Evidence from the other party's think tank lowers the chance that staff side with the requester (a penalty about twice the aligned benefit). Republican staff also rate presenters of center-left evidence as less representative of their district.
evidence.system_side: Cross-party pro cues pass through sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v). Cues between members who are not bridge-builders fall to about 0, and the term is clamped at 0, 'never negative — backfire magnitude not invented' (Bakker-Lelkes-Malka).
evidence.transfer: Directionally, this backs a non-positive out-party cue, and it hints that a negative (backfire) term could be defended. The evidence is about outside information sources judged by staff, not Member-to-Member cosponsor cues, and it is stated intention from an underpowered design. It does not justify inventing a backfire magnitude. Keeping the clamp at 0 remains the conservative reading.

evidence.title: Identifying hidden coalitions in the US House of Representatives by optimally partitioning signed networks based on generalized balance
evidence.claim: The third coalition's median ideology shifts across sessions: very liberal (98th-102nd), center-left (103rd, 111th), center-right (105th-110th). Its members are effective. The paper does not measure persuadability, vote change or electoral vulnerability.
evidence.system_side: PERS is a fixed table over stance tiers (Highly Persuadable 0.65 ... Opponent 0.08; PERS_NONE 0.45).
evidence.transfer: The paper gives no support for the PERS values or for treating third-coalition or Fitzpatrick-type members as more movable. Coalition-level ideological fluidity describes session-to-session composition, not the responsiveness of any individual member.

evidence.title: The Effects of Firms' Lobbying on Resource Misallocation
evidence.claim: The return to lobbying is measured as firm revenue (IV elasticity 0.227 to 0.319), not as member votes or positions (Table 2, printed p.26). Lobbying spend is more than six times PAC, party and candidate contributions on average (Fact 2 and Figure 1, printed pp.8-9; FEC two-year cycles 1999-2016; individual contributions excluded).
evidence.system_side: pflip combines saturating money terms for CU and industry dollars, from congestion.json, with industry = banks plus finserv money, plus peer proximity, at WM 0.35 and WP 0.65. No lobbying spend enters the flip model.
evidence.transfer: The paper has no member-level outcome and cannot calibrate WM, HALFF or the saturation. Its only relevance is the scale fact that lobbying is the largest corporate political channel and is absent from the money terms. Under D-021 that absence is deliberate, so this is not a recommendation to add LDA dollars. The claim that Paul's positions cite H&K under the flip model is not supported by this item (paul_entries holds no takeaways or links), so it was not verified.

evidence.title: Mathematical Modeling, Analysis and Simulation Utilizing Machine Learning Tools for Assessing the Impact of Climate Lobbying
evidence.claim: Only undecided centrists (C) move. Committed Y and N legislators are absorbing states, and the equilibrium with all members undecided is unstable. Widening the centrist band on a -1 to 1 ideology scale from ±0.25 to ±0.35 reverses the House result so that no votes exceed yes votes.
evidence.system_side: PERS assigns committed tiers near-zero persuadability (Champion 0.10, Defender 0.12, Opponent 0.08) and middle tiers the highest (Highly Persuadable 0.65). Silent members get PERS_NONE 0.45; per the flip_model comment, silent cells are 59.8% of matrix cells. Tiers are based on stance, not ideology.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports the extremes being near-fixed only because its model assumes it; Y and N are absorbing by construction. It does not test an inverted-U. Its centrist group is defined by an unnamed ideology scale, while PERS is defined by CU stance tier, so the band result carries over only as a warning: how the movable set is defined can decide the outcome. The system's PERS_NONE sweep shows the same thing in the system itself. Evidence is a single bill (ACESA, 2009) at the federal level.

evidence.title: Mathematical Modeling, Analysis and Simulation Utilizing Machine Learning Tools for Assessing the Impact of Climate Lobbying
evidence.claim: With parameters taken from cited literature and databases (none fitted to the vote), adding donations to the House run moves 1 legislator (230 to 231 yes, 8 undecided). The lobbying run yields 231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided; the authors describe this as undecided members falling from 9 to 1 and conclude that lobbying sways undecided members more than donations do.
evidence.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), with a saturating FEC-money term weighted WM 0.35 and a peer-proximity term weighted WP 0.65. Money is treated as the minority channel. The model has no lobbying-contact channel; money means campaign receipts only.
evidence.transfer: Directionally consistent with the claim that money moves votes little, but this is a contrast between simulation runs under chosen inputs, not an estimated effect. The firm-value inputs (rho_Y, rho_N, Delta pi) are not reported in Table 2, the effect is 7-8 of 435 members on one bill (House, ACESA 2009), and the lobbying input is a ProPublica count of all ACESA-related lobbyists (regular plus a revolving-door subgroup, Fig 3 caption). The paper gives no basis for setting WM/WP or for adding a lobbying channel. Under D-021, LDA-derived lobbying data cannot become an edge or weight term.

evidence.title: Mathematical Modeling, Analysis and Simulation Utilizing Machine Learning Tools for Assessing the Impact of Climate Lobbying
evidence.claim: Campaign donations alone move one House member out of 435 (from 9 undecided to 8, 230 to 231 yes). The Senate is reported only for the combined lobbying-plus-donations run, which changes it by one senator (52/47/1 to 52/48/0). The authors note that donations may reflect ideology rather than buy influence (citing Bonica [5]).
evidence.system_side: MAXSHIFT was cut from 40 to 18 on the premise that money moves positions little, so money-triggered defections are rare and need about a sixth of a member's receipts. Champion and Opponent tiers are immune (COMMITTED set).
evidence.transfer: This is a consistency check, not a calibration. The donation effect in the paper is a model output from literature parameters (I_F, I_A taken from Meng and Rode), not an observed shift. It is weaker than the experimental and null-result literature already cited at money_response.py:15.

evidence.title: Image as Data: Automated Content Analysis for Visual Presentations of Political Actors and Events
evidence.claim: The paper links consistent frames to policy response only by citing Wouters & Walgrave (2017) and Ketelaars et al. (2017), saying higher duplication may indicate greater frame alignment; Study 2 is descriptive and does not test whether higher duplication produces larger effects.
evidence.system_side: Under `--intensity auto`, campaign intensity = 0.5 + alignment in [0.5, 1.5], read from frame_alignment.json; the docstring cites 'our CU Tax Status at 65%'. The chain runs `salience_shock.py --advise` with the default intensity '1.0', so the alignment input does not reach the chain's advisory. frame_alignment.py itself is not in run_pipeline.py; frame_alignment.json was last written 2026-07-01.
evidence.transfer: The 0.5 + alignment mapping has no estimate behind it in Joo, and the 65% input is inflated by ACU syndication. If auto intensity is ever enabled it needs the own-domain recompute first and should be treated as uncalibrated owner judgment.

evidence.title: Measuring Politicians' Public Personality Traits Using Computational Text Analysis: A Multimethod Feasibility Study for Agency and Communion
evidence.claim: The construct is the projected public persona under a lens model. The authors state that the relative weight of intrinsic personality and strategic self-presentation in any cue cannot be determined. The paper reports no behavioural outcome linking agency or communion to responsiveness or persuadability.
evidence.system_side: receptivity_layer.py computes persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) - .40 z(agency) over all members with at least 15 classified sentences, z-scored across parties together (lines 150-155), and blends it at PERSONA_W 0.30 (lines 147, 191). Comments at lines 140-142 cite the cue shares next to the Byrne-style mapping.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports measuring the projected persona only. The communion-to-susceptibility direction and the .60/.40 weights are design priors (Byrne-style), not findings of this paper. The PERSONA_W keep ruling belongs to the owner and is not revisited here.

evidence.title: Measuring Elite Personality Using Speech
evidence.claim: Conscientiousness acts like a discount factor (fn 35), but fn 35 attributes that model to a separate Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh 2015 manuscript. Within this paper, more Conscientious minority members are less deterred by partisan obstacles because they weight future payoffs (pp.15-16); the C effect is smallest for the majority (p.18).
evidence.system_side: receptivity_layer.py: behavioural basis SUSC_z = .40 coop + .30 N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance (line 173); lexical basis .40 A + .30 N - .20 C - .10 E (line 186). Neither branch has a majority-status term. The code comment calls the weights local calibration, not a design prior.
evidence.transfer: The paper concerns bill-type choice, not response to lobbying pressure, so transfer is analogical. Conditioning C on majority status would be a new proposal with no validation behind it.

evidence.title: Influence maximization in social networks using graph embedding and graph neural network
evidence.claim: Training labels are each node's individual influence computed under SIR and IC diffusion, and the seed set is the top k nodes by predicted influence. The preview does not say the simulations are single-source, and the paper does not model competition between seed sets.
evidence.system_side: The cascade is a two-colour first-to-reach race: a node takes the colour of the first neighbour that reaches it, and spread counts only A-coloured activations. Pro seeds (Aseed) are A and anti seeds form the opposing set. Neutral bystanders are activated with probability min(0.9, ind/400000), which is a money-tied activation rather than a fixed-probability cascade.
evidence.transfer: Single-colour standalone-spread labels do not encode competition or seed overlap. A surrogate would need retraining on competitive-race marginal labels before standing in for this engine, and the paper never tests that case.

evidence.title: Social Network Analysis: An Approach and Technique for the Study of Information Exchange
evidence.claim: Citing Coleman, Katz and Menzel (1966): some sources inform (mass media, drug salesmen) while others legitimate adoption; the legitimating sources, other doctors, were most influential, and close reciprocated ties carried legitimacy. Citing Granovetter (1973): over 80 percent of job information came from occasional or rare contacts, under 17 percent from frequent contacts.
evidence.system_side: cpf_diffusion is 1.0 within party and 0.4+0.6*sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v) across party. cpf_pressure is 1.7 co-partisan and 0.5 across party. Both feed p = x/(x+6) on the adjacency passed in.
evidence.transfer: Conceptual parallel only. The cited evidence concerns physicians and job seekers, not legislators, and the article gives no Coleman sample size or data-collection dates. It supports separating an information channel from a legitimation channel. It does not support the 1.7 and 0.5 ratios, the 0.4 floor or the constant 6. Coleman's reciprocated ties must not be imported as a reciprocity weight, since reciprocity is not validated (D-104 to D-108).

evidence.title: Big data-assisted social media analytics for business model for business decision making system competitive analysis
evidence.claim: Defines a time-varying event hotness index He(t) = sum over bursting events of sentiment x volume, with bursts flagged by z-scores of one-day variation over trailing 5- and 25-day windows (|z|>30). It is proposed as a brand-value measure, and no estimates or forecast errors are reported.
evidence.system_side: Salience parameters (partisan gap z_c, policy uncertainty psi_c, backfire b) are estimated from the static stance matrix. There is no time-series trigger for when an issue becomes salient. Go-public advice is computed per issue, not per moment.
evidence.transfer: A burst detector on press and social volume per CU category could supply a dated salience-onset signal. Any such signal stays UNVERIFIED until it is tested against Noble-Turner style co-partisan shifts on a second path. The paper's 'sentiment x volume' must not be imported as an influence or importance score: it measures volume, not access or influence. It comes from consumer tweets about retailers, not congressional statements.

evidence.title: The (Financial) Ties That Bind: Social Networks of Intraparty Caucuses
evidence.claim: Vulnerable members (Cook PVI likely, Oct 2018, dichotomous) are about 70% (R) and 75% (D) more likely to receive a member-to-member LPAC tie, per the text. Republican leaders give to vulnerable members at 73% (Table 4 coef 1.004***). 115th Congress, stratified by party; denominators 238 R and 168 D connected nodes (Table 2-3 notes).
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + COMPET_AMPLITUDE*exp(-max(lean,0)/COMPET_SCALE), AMPLITUDE 1.0 and SCALE 5.0. lean is Cook PVI points toward the member's party. Scales effective dollars on both money legs. Code comment marks AMPLITUDE and SCALE as judgment constants and the reciprocity as not validated.
evidence.transfer: Paper is evidence on where donor LPAC money goes (binary tie presence, Oct 2018 dichotomy, member-to-member only). It does not show a dollar buys more in a competitive seat, which c encodes. It supports Cook PVI as the signal donors act on, not the continuous exp(-lean/5) decay. Neither validates nor refutes D-104..D-108.

evidence.title: The (Financial) Ties That Bind: Social Networks of Intraparty Caucuses
evidence.claim: Vulnerability is associated with higher inward LPAC degree, for both raw and weighted degree, from a regression reported in the text. Leadership is associated with higher outward degree. Givers target electorally exposed co-partisans.
evidence.system_side: leverage = 1 + LELEV*(1 - security), LELEV default 0.8, security is a percentile of the Ballotpedia Election_Average, with unmatched members set to neutral 0.5.
evidence.transfer: Backs vulnerability as a magnet for co-partisan money, consistent with defend plays. Gives no evidence that competitive seats are cheaper to move. The paper uses Cook PVI while this component uses Ballotpedia Election_Average, so two vulnerability measures feed the engine. Applies within party only.

evidence.title: The (Financial) Ties That Bind: Social Networks of Intraparty Caucuses
evidence.claim: Within a party, Model A (both members in the same caucus) is positive for Freedom +1.208*** and Tea Party +0.686*** (R), and Progressive +0.381* (D, p<0.1). It is negative for Tuesday Group -1.033*** and Liberty -0.389*. Model D (recipient in caucus, donor not) is -1.020*** for Freedom and -0.545*** for Tea Party. Model C (donor in caucus, recipient not) is -1.780*** for Freedom and -0.314*** for Tea Party. Mean transitivity R 0.497, D 0.2768.
evidence.system_side: cpf_pressure returns 1.7 for co-partisan pairs, 0.5 for out-partisan pairs, and 1.0 otherwise. cpf_diffusion is 1.0 within party. Every co-partisan is treated alike; there is no intraparty faction term.
evidence.transfer: Evidence is binary LPAC donation ties with amounts ignored, not cosponsorship diffusion or persuasion, so it cannot set a faction multiplier. It shows party is not a homogeneous block for money ties, and the fault line is party-specific: any pooled faction coefficient needs party strata. 115th House primary; 116th replication is partial (Tables A1-A4).

evidence.title: The (Financial) Ties That Bind: Social Networks of Intraparty Caucuses
evidence.claim: Announced retirees are about 40% (R) and 45% (D) less likely to receive member LPAC ties. Republican leaders give to retirees at 39% (Table 4 coef -0.397***). The Table 5 retirement coefficient is -0.055 marked *** with SE 0.102, which is internally inconsistent.
evidence.system_side: incent_mult is 0.60 for retiring members (incent_term returns 0.60 if retiring). With COMPET_MULT on, incent_term_compet still returns 0.60 for retirees, so the final-term factor stays.
evidence.transfer: Shows peers and leaders put less money into retirees, which fits treating retirees as low-value targets. Says nothing about whether retirees respond less to pressure, which is the mechanism the 0.60 factor encodes. The factor still rests on Fouirnaies and Hall, not this paper.

evidence.title: Mapping the Ideological Marketplace
evidence.claim: Table 2 (printed p.20, PDF p.21), individual donors (5,000 random donors with 25+ federal gifts, 2004-2012): LogLik ideological -1334200, partisan electoral -1405855, investor -1504601, baseline -1520312. Ideological fits best of these. Paper says partisanship is a coarsened ideology measure, so party vs ideology variance is hard to separate. Largest shifts in period-specific CFscores from candidate covariates are 0.03 to 0.05, about a twentieth of an SD (supplement Table 1 text). Paper models donor allocation and does not estimate a dollar's effect on the recipient.
evidence.system_side: compet_c(lean) = 1 + COMPET_AMPLITUDE*exp(-max(lean,0)/COMPET_SCALE), AMPLITUDE 1.0, SCALE 5.0. Applied to effective dollars on both money legs. Code calls AMPLITUDE and SCALE uncalibrated owner judgment; reciprocity NOT validated (D-104..D-108).
evidence.transfer: Paper supports neither c nor its calibration: its dependent variable is where individual donors send money, not what a dollar buys in a competitive seat. Sample is individuals 2004-2012 only. Any use of the partisan-electoral result must note that party and ideology are collinear.

evidence.title: Mapping the Ideological Marketplace
evidence.claim: Table 2 (PDF p.21): individuals investor -1504601 vs baseline -1520312 and ideological -1334200. Corporate and trade PACs (N=1312): unconstrained investor -1687949 vs ideological -1694458, so the investor form is ahead by about 6,500 log-lik units. Paper says corporate and trade PACs combine ideological and strategic motives and excludes them from scaling as a precaution. Paper does not measure vote-buying, access or any effect of money.
evidence.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b) when a+b > 0 (flip_model.py:97). a = WM*pm*(c*cu+1)/((c*cu+1)+HALFF*R) + WP*nA/mAt; b has the same form on bank plus finserv money. WM 0.35 and WP 0.65 are labelled CALIBRATED in code with the comment that money buys access and effort more than votes. HALFF default 0.10.
evidence.transfer: Both money legs are corporate or trade PAC money, the class the paper finds mixed-motive, so the individual-donor ideology result cannot be borrowed to call these dollars purely expressive. Paper provides no calibration of WM, HALFF or MAXSHIFT, so it gives no support for the CALIBRATED label on WM.

evidence.title: Mapping the Ideological Marketplace
evidence.claim: Text PDF p.20: the partisan electoral model's main implication is that donors fund competitive races to maximize party seat share. Table 2 (PDF p.21): for individuals partisan -1405855 vs ideological -1334200, so the partisan electoral model fits worse. Paper also says the ideological model significantly improves fit over a partisan model.
evidence.system_side: comp = round(1 - security, 3) from Ballotpedia security. Defend value = comp times the mean positive stance gap vs cross-party challenger. Contest general route is multiplied by comp; contest primary route is not. No money term in the play formula.
evidence.transfer: The paper states a hypothesis it rejects for individual donors; it neither supports nor refutes the comp weighting. It describes donor allocation, not the payoff of a play.

evidence.title: Influencing Connected Legislators
evidence.claim: Legislators value conformity with network peers, so a group pricing a legislator counts downstream effects through network walks (Bonacich multiplier), not only the legislator's own vote (Sec 2; Prop 1). The estimated externality is positive and significant: phi 0.2088 committee, 0.0837 alumni (Table 2).
evidence.system_side: flip_model.py pflip adds a one-hop peer term WP*nA/mAt where nA counts only neighbours in the pro camp, so a CU dollar to member m changes only m's own pflip. Neighbours change only when a conversion updates camp; optimize.py 136-144 then clears the cache with fm._cache.clear() and recomputes proximity.
evidence.transfer: The paper's phi measures network autocorrelation in contributions, which may reflect correlated effects rather than vote conformity; the paper does not show that money to one member moves a peer's vote. The paper's equilibrium is two-sided; the system optimizes for one PAC, so the link is conceptual. Any continuous spillover term needs its own prereg look, not a calibration from this paper.

evidence.title: Systemic and Sequential Links between Campaign Donations and Lobbying
evidence.claim: Corporate PAC donations show the strongest association with later lobbying of the recipient (committee 0.103 to 0.147 versus CEO 0.017 to 0.050 and employee 0.015 to 0.039). The authors say the estimates should not be read as causal (p.29). The amount effect is small: 0.003 on log donation amount in the firm-politician FE column (Table 1 col.8), which is about 0.03 pp per 10 percent (text p.20).
evidence.system_side: fec/engine/flip_model.py line 21 sets WM and WP to 0.35 and 0.65 and comments that money is the minority partner to peer and network influence. Engine money is direct-PAC only (fec/collect/refresh_fec_money.py docstring, individual contributions out of scope).
evidence.transfer: The paper says nothing about the WM to WP ratio or roll-call flips. Its outcome is the firm's lobbying behaviour, not the member's vote, in manufacturing firms 2008-2018. It supports at most the general premise that PAC money is the most-associated channel, so it is context and a weak prior, not evidence for the 0.35 weight.

evidence.title: Campaign Contributions Facilitate Access to Congressional Officials: A Randomized Field Experiment
evidence.claim: Donor label raised senior access in 191 House offices of one party, June to August 2013: chief of staff or above 12.5% vs 2.4% (p=.006), legislative director or above 18.8% vs 5.5% (p=.005), Member 7.8% vs 2.4% (p=.07). Ratios implied by Table 1: about 5.2, 3.4 and 3.2. The paper reports no effect on votes or positions.
evidence.system_side: pflip(n) = a/(a+b) at flip_model.py:92-96 puts a saturating CU-money term with WM 0.35 directly into a member's flip probability, against a peer term with WP 0.65. The CALIBRATED comment at flip_model.py:21 lists Kalla and Broockman among sources for money buys access/effort greater than votes.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports only the access step: one 2013 experiment, one liberal group, one bill, one party's House offices, a randomized donor label rather than dollars. It gives no estimate of WM, WP, HALFF or saturation, and no effect on votes or positions (p.555). The citation supports access before votes only if narrowed to access; the not-votes half is outside the paper.

evidence.title: Campaign Contributions Facilitate Access to Congressional Officials: A Randomized Field Experiment
evidence.claim: Offices were blocked on Obama's 2012 two-party vote share among six covariates, with omnibus balance p=.92 (chi-square 1.44, 5 df). The paper reports no heterogeneity of the donor-label effect by seat competitiveness.
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + AMPLITUDE*exp(-max(lean,0)/SCALE) multiplies effective dollars on both money legs. AMPLITUDE = 1.0 and SCALE = 5.0 are judgment constants, labeled uncalibrated, and the reciprocity they encode is not validated.
evidence.transfer: Blocking on partisanship balances it across arms but does not estimate whether the donor effect differs in competitive seats; 64 treated offices could not have estimated that. The paper gives no support for c. The multiplier stays unvalidated (D-104..D-108).

evidence.title: Campaign Contributions Facilitate Access to Congressional Officials: A Randomized Field Experiment
evidence.claim: The measured outcome was access: the rank of the official who attended. Positions and votes were not measured. Cosponsorship was nine legislators in total, with equal shares in both arms, and the authors say it tells little about effects.
evidence.system_side: MAXSHIFT = 18, labeled CALIBRATED from 40 on the premise that money moves positions little and buys access and effort, not votes (money_response.py:15-17). LOSSFRAME = 1.10 treats competitor spending as a loss frame (money_response.py:31). The code cites Ansolabehere and Fowler-Garro-Spenkuch for this premise, not this paper.
evidence.transfer: The paper can be cited for the access measure, but not for a null on positions: its cosponsorship estimate is uninformative rather than null. It says nothing about MAXSHIFT, HALF, DTHRESH or LOSSFRAME. The not-votes half of the premise lies outside the paper (p.555).

evidence.title: Lobbying ROI: An Analysis under the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004 (also: Measuring Rates of Return for Lobbying Expenditures)
evidence.claim: Lobbying firms repatriated about 70% of dollars: 209.1bn of 298.36bn (Table 6; the introduction says 208bn). Table 5 has no lobbying regressor, so the only lobbying test is the group comparison in Table 6. The introduction promises a regression with lobbying, and no such regression appears in the text.
evidence.system_side: flip_model.py sets WM,WP = 0.35,0.65 and computes pflip as a/(a+b), where the money term saturates against receipts (HALFF times R). A grep of the file finds no reference to lobbying expenditure, so the model takes no lobbying input.
evidence.transfer: Does not bear on WM, WP or HALFF. The paper measures a firm benefit, not member movement, and measures lobbying rather than PAC giving. Furnas (item furnas-nd-conflating-lobbying-pacs) finds only a small minority of organizations do both. The paper gives no basis for raising the money weight. The clause about Paul's ROI enthusiasm has no support in the item file and is dropped.

evidence.title: Who chokes under pressure? The Big Five personality traits and decision-making under pressure
evidence.claim: Neuroticism was the only trait significant in the regression in both experiments. Exp 1: condition x N b = .45, p = .02 (minus sign lost in text extraction; authors describe a negative effect), interaction DR2 = .06, F(11,115) = 1.96, p = .04; under high pressure N b = .50, p < .01; under low pressure ns. Exp 2 (social plus time pressure, no low-pressure arm): N b = .31, p < .05; A b = .36, p < .01; model R2 = .19. Exp 1 agreeableness interaction only a trend, b = .33, p = .08. Authors call the agreeableness result exploratory.
evidence.system_side: The susceptibility composite weights A at .40 and N at .30 (comment: 'A ranked above N per the user's framing'). The docstring says high A adds to N-driven choking 'under social pressure (their Exp-2 interaction)'. Exp 2 has no low-pressure arm, so it cannot show an interaction. The default behavioural basis fills the A slot with cooperation_v2 (share-based; code comment gives rho +0.888 with bpf), not trait agreeableness. susc drives susc_mult [0.70, 1.30] and edge_mult [0.80, 1.20].
evidence.transfer: Weak transfer. (1) Construct: the outcome is worse choices on a delayed-reward lab task, not being moved by a persuader. (2) Population: undergraduates earning course credit at one university, individual decisions, an $8 bonus; not legislators facing lobbyists. (3) Measurement: the paper uses self-report BFI; the system uses text or behavioural proxies (affective_n for N, cooperation_v2 for A). (4) Size: Exp 1 step-1 R2 = .10 (condition plus five traits); the interaction increment is DR2 = .06, so the paper gives no anchor for the plus or minus 30 percent multiplier range. The paper supports the direction of an N-under-pressure term only; it does not support A outweighing N or the size of the term.

evidence.title: Who chokes under pressure? The Big Five personality traits and decision-making under pressure
evidence.claim: Under high pressure conscientiousness correlated negatively with performance, r = .27, p < .05 (Exp 1 correlation only). In the Exp 1 regression it was a trend, b = .16, p = .09. Experiment 2 found C not predictive: r = .16 ns, and Table 5 gives b = .16 with no significance mark. Authors say no clear conclusion about conscientiousness is possible. Extraversion and openness had no effect in either experiment.
evidence.system_side: The composite subtracts .20 x C and .10 x E, so high-C and high-E members count as less susceptible (lines 186 and 189). The docstring at lines 9-10 says these dampeners are design priors, not Byrne findings.
evidence.transfer: The paper's C direction is opposite to the code's dampener sign, but the only evidence is one uncontrolled correlation that the authors decline to interpret and that did not replicate. That qualifies the term; it does not contradict it. For C and E, the honest wording is that this paper gives no support to the dampener.

evidence.title: The influence of personality traits on the effect of persuasion strategies: A systematic literature review
evidence.claim: Count-based susceptibility ranking across 80 studies: agreeableness High, extraversion Above average, conscientiousness Average, openness Below average, neuroticism Low (least susceptible). No pooled effect sizes.
evidence.system_side: The susceptibility composite has the same structure on both bases. Lexical basis: susc_trait = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E. Live default (RECEPT_TRAITS=behavioral, RECEPT_N=affective, RECEPT_COOP=v2): .40 coop_v2 + .30 affective_N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance. The code cites Byrne 2015 choking-under-pressure for N, and states that the C and E dampeners are design priors, not Byrne findings.
evidence.transfer: Weak transfer. The review measures response to persuasion messages in consumers and students, using self-reported traits and perceived-persuasiveness outcomes in health and tech settings. The system's N slot is choking under pressure (Byrne), a different construct, and members' traits are read from text or behaviour, not self-report. The review supports the positive A or cooperation weight. It cuts against the positive N weight and gives no support to the negative E or dominance weight. It cannot set magnitudes because it reports no effect sizes. Neither sign change is recommended on this evidence alone: changing weights moves ranks and is a gated recalibration, which is Paul's call.

evidence.title: The influence of personality traits on the effect of persuasion strategies: A systematic literature review
evidence.claim: Neuroticism is the least susceptible trait overall, yet Oyibo & Vassileva (2019) found it the trait most consistently correlated with responsiveness to social-influence strategies, and Gkika et al. (2016) found greater acceptance of social proof among high-neuroticism participants.
evidence.system_side: edge_mult is an affine gain on the same susc scalar, applied to cascade receivers (peer or social influence). susc_mult scales pressure and money response. One scalar serves both channels.
evidence.transfer: The paper suggests that the direction of N may differ by channel: positive for peer or social-proof influence, which the edge_mult cascade receiver models, and negative for direct persuasion appeals. That would argue against a single susceptibility dial for both channels. The paper's evidence is one or two persuasive-technology studies, so treat this as a hypothesis only.
