evidence.title: The influence of personality traits on the effect of persuasion strategies: A systematic literature review
evidence.claim: Trait-matched strategies are more effective than non-matching ones, and contra-matched (random, non-ideal) strategies are often counterproductive. Examples: agreeableness with reciprocity and liking; extraversion with liking, commitment, scarcity and reciprocity; neuroticism with commitment and consistency.
evidence.system_side: The engine models one undifferentiated pressure. pressure_mult = clip(susc_mult x incent x pt, 0.50, 1.60), with no strategy or appeal-type dimension, so a mismatch can only reduce gain and never backfire on this channel.
evidence.transfer: This only applies if lobbying asks were coded by appeal type, and the system has no such data. The matching evidence comes from health and persuasive-technology apps, with outcomes mostly measured as perceived persuasiveness rather than behaviour (Sec 5.3). Cialdini's 'reciprocity' here is a message strategy. It is unrelated to the system's unvalidated reciprocity assumption (D-104..D-108).

evidence.title: Efficient Influence Maximization in Social-Networks Under Independent Cascade Model
evidence.claim: Structure-derived edge probabilities p_ij = 0.01 + (d_i+d_j)/n + CN(i,j)/n raise spread for every algorithm on the co-authorship graphs, e.g. Degree +32.60% (NetPhy, k=20) and CELF +55.55% (NetPhy, k=10). The form is asserted to reflect real propagation dynamics and is not fitted to or validated against observed diffusion.
evidence.system_side: build_P sets p(u to v) = x/(x+6) with x = cosponsor weight times cpf_diffusion(u,v) times the receiver edge_mult term. The constant 6 is a fixed design value in code, not estimated. Verified.
evidence.transfer: The paper gives no calibration or validation, so it cannot support tuning or replacing the constant 6. Its gains are percent increases over a 0.01 baseline that it says gives very little influence and does not favour real-world dynamics; calling the gains mechanical is this analysis's reading, not the paper's. The common-neighbour term is a candidate covariate only. The degree term raises probability for hubs and must not be presented as support for the REJECTED per-edge volume normalization.

evidence.title: Adaptive Submodularity: Theory and Applications in Active Learning and Stochastic Optimization
evidence.claim: Stochastic submodular maximization with independent item states (failure types) and a monotone submodular objective: greedy obtains (1-1/e) of the best adaptive policy (Thm 16, generalizing Asadpour et al. 2008). Robustness to a misspecified prior is shown for a multiplicative error condition with alpha = d/c (Sec 4.3).
evidence.system_side: Each lobbied seed activates independently with probability gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob x SGATE[tier]). Draws use a dedicated CRN key range offset by 2^62. SGATE runs from 1.00 (Highly Persuadable) to 0.35 (Opponent) as design constants; unlisted tiers default to 0.85.
evidence.transfer: The structure matches: independent per-seed Bernoulli take-up over a spread function. The guarantee also needs spread given activated seeds to be monotone submodular, which is not shown for this competitive kernel, and needs known take-up probabilities. SGATE and seed_prob are unestimated, so the known-prior assumption fails.

evidence.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
evidence.claim: The strongest self-report category effects sit at |rho| .08-.14 (abstract p. 843), and the 52 categories explain 5.07 percent of self-report variance (Table 4 p. 854). Effects are typically stronger for longer texts (Table 6 continuous moderators, p. 854).
evidence.system_side: Default basis is behavioral (RECEPT_TRAITS default). The lexical fallback is susc = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E. Shrinkage is min(1, sqrt(tokens/1500)). Code and comments match the rel. The sqrt form is not estimated by this paper.
evidence.transfer: Closed-vocabulary rates carry little true trait variance, so a lexical composite is mostly noise. This supports keeping the lexical basis out of the default, but not the specific sqrt shrinkage form.

evidence.title: Optimal Targeting in Fundraising: A Causal Machine-Learning Approach
evidence.claim: Responsiveness to the gift is heterogeneous and has to be estimated. Causal-forest best linear predictor heterogeneity loading 0.959 (SE 0.710; p 0.088 one-sided) on the warm list and 0.511 (SE 1.069) on the cold list (Table E.3). The 2014 rule applied to a caliper-matched 2015 warm-list sample (radius 0.1, 35.6 percent treated) gave +2.64 vs all-gift and +2.30 vs no-gift. On the full 2015 sample it gave no significant gain. The paper reports significance against no-gift up to caliper radius 0.25 and says effects are not significant above radius 0.1.
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0), with lean = Cook PVI points toward the member's own party (function compet_c). It multiplies effective dollars on both money legs of the flip family; the per-member cap and the pot stay real dollars. The code labels the constants as owner judgment, uncalibrated, with the reciprocity they encode not validated. The dial defaults ON (unset means ON; '0' reverts).
evidence.transfer: The paper is about method, not legislators or PVI. It shows what establishing heterogeneous dollar effectiveness would require: randomized variation, a heterogeneity test and a transfer check to a new population. It gives no evidence for or against the PVI shape of c. Do not cite it as support for c.

evidence.title: Adversarial Attack on Graph Neural Networks as An Influence Maximization Problem
evidence.claim: Proposition 2: if each threshold CDF F_j is concave on [0, +inf), the expected spread h(S) is submodular, so greedy selection applies. Corollary 1 (uniform thresholds, Eq. 6) gives a saturated coverage objective that is submodular. Lemma 1: influence maximization on the directed bipartite linear threshold graph is NP-hard, by reduction from Set Cover with thresholds alpha/2.
evidence.system_side: lt_priming THETA ladder: deterministic constants from 0.6 (Highly Persuadable) to 3.0 (Opponent). prime() adds net_lean/120 and 0.25 per declared Opponent cell, sums P[u][v] times xf over pro sources, and solves each target separately for the cheapest mix of recruits and money. No seed-set objective is optimized.
evidence.transfer: The concavity result transfers as mathematics only. Lemma 1 is an NP-hardness result for deterministic thresholds; the paper does not state a converse that missing concavity implies hardness. A point-mass (step) threshold CDF is not concave on [0, +inf), so the paper's submodularity guarantee does not cover lt_priming's deterministic thresholds if they were aggregated into a seed-set objective. Moderate for the mathematics, weak for empirical relevance.

evidence.title: Twenty Years of Personality Computing: Threats, Challenges and Future Directions
evidence.claim: Computer Perception convergent validity is Rho 0.30 (Hinds and Joinson 2024). The paper names personality-aware marketing used to influence voting (cites [79]) as a threat and calls for explainable AI in Perception systems.
evidence.system_side: receptivity_layer.py computes susceptibility as .40 coop + .30 N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance under the default behavioral basis, blended with the persona channel at PERSONA_W (default 0.30); RECEPT_TRAITS=lexical reverts to .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E.
evidence.transfer: The 0.30 figure is a Perception convergent validity, not a Recognition figure; the bearing's earlier wording implied otherwise. The 9 percent shared variance is the reviewer's arithmetic, not the paper's. The voting threat concerns voters and consumers, so it is context for wording, not evidence against the layer. Owner ruling on PERSONA_W was not checked.

evidence.title: RELINK: Edge Activation for Closed Network Influence Maximization via Deep Reinforcement Learning
evidence.claim: Spread is estimated with 100,000 Monte Carlo IC simulations per selected subgraph, each experiment repeated 10 times, with averages reported (Sec 6.1). The paper gives no rationale for the number of draws. The 0.85 to 1.15 range is only the colour scale of the Fig 6 heatmap, not a claim about resolving method differences.
evidence.system_side: Competitive IC uses keyed splitmix64 common random numbers (sm64 in moneyball_core.py around lines 549-553; build_P lines 555-562). MC default is 20 in budget_frontier.py line 7 and 40 in cosponsor_route.py line 25. The scenario MC setting was not checked.
evidence.transfer: The paper's 100,000 draws are its own protocol and say nothing on whether 20 to 40 draws are adequate for Melange rank decisions. Adequacy remains the system's own claim (mc_stability_check), which this paper does not test. Any variance-reduction benefit of CRN is not supported by this paper.

evidence.title: Understanding Partisan Cue Receptivity: Tests of Predictions from the Bounded Rationality and Expressive Utility Perspectives
evidence.claim: Out-party cues lower policy support by about .06 (study 1, p < .01, N = 747), about .07 (study 2, no p-value stated in the text) and about .07 in the pooled studies 1-4 meta-analysis (no p-value stated). In-party cues add about .03, non-significant in studies 1 and 2 and reported without a test in the pooled model. The out-party sign is negative, so the paper supports no positive out-partisan persuasion weight.
evidence.system_side: cpf_pressure in fec/moneyball_core.py returns 1.7 for co-partisan pairs, 0.5 for cross-party D/R pairs and 1.0 otherwise; the docstring at line 11 cites Furnas/Bakker source-alignment. fec/engine/flip_model.py line 58 binds it, and lines 138-139 sum pro-campaign neighbours into nA and anti neighbours into nB, both weighted by cpf, so an out-party pro-CU neighbour adds positive pull at weight 0.5. The dashboard align() at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl line 585 returns SRCPRO/SRCANTI; the constant values were not checked.
evidence.transfer: Direction only. The paper measures mass-public 0-1 policy support after one embedded cue, on low-salience issues, in 2016-2018 non-probability online panels. It does not measure legislator-to-legislator pressure, cosponsorship or lobbying. The sign result supports zeroing or reversing the out-partisan weight, not the 1.7 amplification, since the paper's in-party effect is small and often null. Legislator-side constants need elite cue evidence such as Box-Steffensmeier et al.

evidence.title: Understanding Partisan Cue Receptivity: Tests of Predictions from the Bounded Rationality and Expressive Utility Perspectives
evidence.claim: Out-party cues lower policy support by about .07 on a 0-1 scale in the pooled studies 1-4 analysis, relative to the no-cue control. The paper does not use the word backfire; the decrease is the reported effect. Heterogeneity runs through partisan identity strength interacted with cognitive resources (NfC, latent resources). The paper measures no bipartisan-bridge or cross-party attribute. The authors say real messages often carry both in-party and out-party cues.
evidence.system_side: BAKKER_XCUE defaults to on (fec/engine/lt_priming.py line 63, env default '1'). xf(u,v) at line 64 returns 1.0 for same-party pairs and sqrt(bpf_u times bpf_v) for cross-party pairs, so a cross-party pro-cue is scaled by bridge share and is never negative. xf is applied in the pressure sum (line 103) and in the recruit candidate terms (lines 131 and 133). The dashboard port at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl line 630 mirrors it.
evidence.transfer: Sign only. The paper supports shrinking out-party cross-cues toward zero, which the bpf scaling does. The paper does not support the bridge exemption, under which sqrt(bpf) restores full cross-party influence for perfect bridge pairs, because bipartisanship is never measured. Mass-public one-shot survey effects do not transfer to elite cosponsorship recruitment without elite-level evidence.

evidence.title: Understanding Partisan Cue Receptivity: Tests of Predictions from the Bounded Rationality and Expressive Utility Perspectives
evidence.claim: Out-party cues lower support by about .06 to .07 and in-party cues raise it by about .03 (pooled and studies 1-2). The authors speculate, post hoc, that in-party patterns were stronger in the food irradiation (change) studies and out-party patterns in the farm subsidy (status quo) studies, and name other possible explanations.
evidence.system_side: salience_shock.py steps_for (lines 99-111): the retreat regime gives co-partisans +1 and out-partisans -1; rally gives co-partisans +1 and out-partisans +0.5 only when bpf is at least 0.30; backfire gives out-partisans -1. These are sign-and-unit steps before intensity and susceptibility scaling. The dashboard efm() at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl lines 659-660 applies the oppose and support multipliers, and its comment at lines 655-656 cites Lee 2009, not Bakker or Furnas.
evidence.transfer: The paper's mass-level out-party repulsion supports the negative out-partisan step in retreat and backfire. It shows no positive out-party movement, so it does not back the rally +0.5 step, which must rest on other sources. The issue-dependence finding is post hoc and should not be used to select a regime.

evidence.title: Understanding Partisan Cue Receptivity: Tests of Predictions from the Bounded Rationality and Expressive Utility Perspectives
evidence.claim: Cue receptivity is not higher among low-resource people; the meta-analysis shows no larger cue effects for low resources. Among high-resource respondents the in-party cue effect rises with partisan identity strength: meta slopes CRT b=.09 (SE .04), NfC b=.15 (SE .05), latent b=.15 (SE .05). The roughly 15-percentage-point rise from lowest to highest identity strength is reported for latent resources only.
evidence.system_side: receptivity_layer.py lines 173-191: susc_trait = .40 cooperation_v2 + .30 N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance (line 186), described in the module docstring (lines 6-9) as a design prior and not a Byrne finding. The final susceptibility is (1 minus PW) times susc_trait plus PW times the persona z, with PW from PERSONA_W defaulting to 0.30 (line 147). The persona z uses communion and agency, not partisan identity, so the layer has no partisan identity strength term. cooperation_v2 is a cross-party share that the file notes is near-duplicate of bpf (rho +0.888).
evidence.transfer: Weak. The paper studies the mass public; legislators are high-resource and strongly identified, so the moderator has little range in Congress. The paper concerns party cues, not lobbying pressure. The layer's design prior does not come from this paper. UNVERIFIED agent analysis (DE-062).

evidence.title: Predicting the Big 5 personality traits from digital footprints on social media: A meta-analysis
evidence.claim: Agreeableness is the least recoverable trait from footprints (r .29 [.21,.36]). A gained no accuracy from multiple footprint types. Among the moderators tested, demographics was the only significant gain for A (beta .25, R2 .19).
evidence.system_side: Lexical susceptibility formula is susc = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E (receptivity_layer.py line 189). The default behavioral basis uses .40*coop + .30*reactivity N - .20*dil - .10*dom (line 186). The BASIS comment (lines 58-65) documents that RECEPT_TRAITS=lexical reverts the basis; the default is behavioral.
evidence.transfer: The paper is about predicting self-report among lay users. It does not test susceptibility to pressure or any choking composite, so it cannot support the susceptibility weights. Its only bearing is that lexical A is the weakest footprint trait. The analyst's statement that the paper supports the system's move from lexical A to behavioral cooperation is the analyst's inference, not the paper's finding.

evidence.title: Do Redistricting Commissions Avoid Partisan Gerrymanders?
evidence.claim: District partisanship is partly a product of how lines are drawn. Compared with 10,000 neutral plans per state, enacted maps added about +1.5 points of pro-Democratic asymmetry (median minus mean) in Arizona, 1.7-3.7 points against Democrats in New Jersey and 2.7-4.0 points against Democrats in Virginia (10 of 10 elections; fewer than 1% of neutral plans as skewed). The Arizona commission's districts had larger SDs than expected, meaning packing in both directions and fewer competitive seats than neutral drawing would produce.
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0), where lean is the Cook PVI oriented toward the member's party. c scales effective dollars on both money legs. Ten mid-decade redistricted states and PVI shifts of 5 points or more are flagged but never altered. AMPLITUDE and SCALE are uncalibrated owner judgment, and the reciprocity they encode is not validated.
evidence.transfer: The paper's shifts are state-level skews in two-party vote share. They are not per-district PVI changes, so they show only the order of magnitude by which a map can move lean. Under the model formula, a 3-4 point lean change moves c by roughly 0.45-0.55 near lean 0. That makes c partly a function of map choice, which matters most in the flagged 2025-26 mid-decade redistricted states. The paper covers the 2010 round and congressional districts only, and it says nothing about whether contributions are worth more in competitive seats. It must not be cited as support for the reciprocity premise (D-104..D-108).

evidence.claim: Among opposing-bloc MEP dyads, higher point connectivity predicts less co-voting. Table 3 model 3 log-odds multilevel coefficient is -0.1020 (SE 0.0307), about 10 percent lower odds per unit (95 percent CI 7-13 percent). Predicted co-voting falls from 52 to 44 percent between connectivity 0.6 and 3.8 (about -1 to +1 SD). Window: 40 Environment Committee roll calls, July 2004 to July 2008. Denominator: 1,319 non-unanimous dyads (perfect co-voters excluded in model 3).
evidence.system_side: cpf_diffusion gives every cross-party edge between D and R members a contagion weight of 0.4 + 0.6*sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), so non-bridge out-party pairs keep a floor of 0.4. build_P maps the weight to activation probability x/(x+6) with x = w*cpf*edge_mult.
evidence.transfer: Paper tie is staff-reported contact, not cosponsorship. Setting is a multi-party EP committee, not two-party US Congress. Result is cross-sectional association with acknowledged simultaneity and specification sensitivity (fn. 81). It does not show cross-party diffusion is zero or negative in US cosponsorship. Use it to motivate a test stratified by party pair, not to change a constant.

evidence.claim: Social connection between political adversaries goes with less voting agreement, not more. Theory predicts this when the pair expects to disagree (H1, Fig. 1). Opposed-bloc baseline co-voting is about 50 percent (p. 626).
evidence.system_side: The BAKKER_XCUE signing passes a cross-party pro-cue through sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), so cues from non-bridge out-partisans fall to about 0. The value is never negative because it is a square root of products of non-negative bridge-factor values. Priming pressure does not treat out-party ties as persuasive.
evidence.transfer: Direction agrees: out-party ties should not count as pro-pressure. The association is not causal and is EP staff contact, so it does not justify adding a negative backfire term. Keeping the floor at 0 remains the default.

evidence.title: Contingency-Aware Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
evidence.claim: A selected seed is willing with a probability q that is known a priori. Footnote 2 says q is the same for all nodes because per-node values are impractical to know. Default q = 0.6; Q3 varies q over 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8. The paper estimates no real-world q.
evidence.system_side: gate(n,cs) = max(0.15, seed_prob(n) x SGATE[stance]) at moneyball_core.py:630. SGATE values at 626-629 match the description (1.00 down to 0.35; unknown 0.85; Ally, Champion, Defender 1.0). seed_prob has a behavioral branch (0.60 + .10 coop + .06 breadth + .04 visibility, clipped 0.30-0.90) and a non-behavioral branch (0.60 + .10A + .06O + .04E, same clip).
evidence.transfer: The modeling idea transfers: invitation is not activation. The paper's q is homogeneous and its analysis is multi-round. SGATE is member-specific and used single-shot, so Theorems 1-3 do not cover it. The 0.60 baseline is the paper's simulation default, not an estimate. The source population is HIV peer leaders, not legislators. SGATE values remain design priors until measured.

evidence.title: Threshold Models for Competitive Influence in Social Networks
evidence.claim: With technology-specific edge weights, the separated-threshold competitive problem (Theorem 7) and the Carnes wave-propagation variant with technology-specific probabilities (Theorem 8) are NP-hard to approximate within Omega(N^(1/2-eps)) by a Vertex Cover reduction (Appendix D, Theorem 16). This refutes the Carnes et al. conjecture for that case.
evidence.system_side: The engine builds one kernel P = build_P(adj) and uses it for both colours (budget_frontier.py 77, per_topic_coalition.py 37, scenario.py 39). Pro and anti frontiers draw the same keyed splitmix value per (iteration, edge) (budget_frontier.py 83-94; per_topic_coalition.py 44-55), and the first colour to reach a node keeps it. The paper states its hardness for models with separate per-technology edge weights, so the shared kernel sits outside that stated scope. The paper does not describe the Bharathi-Kempe-Salek weights, so calling them shared-weight is the analyst reading, not the paper.
evidence.transfer: Holds only while the kernel stays shared. Giving anti-side diffusion its own edge weights or physics, such as cpf_pressure on the B side only (moneyball_core.py 546), would move the engine into the stated hardness scope. Tie-breaking by frontier order is not analysed in this paper.

evidence.title: Threshold Models for Competitive Influence in Social Networks
evidence.claim: In the separated-threshold competitive LT model a node is activated by whichever technology weighted active neighbours first exceed that technology own threshold. Adding A seeds never raises the probability that B propagates (Lemma 3 part 1, used in Theorem 3), but the process is not submodular in general (Theorem 4, counterexample only in an unincluded full version).
evidence.system_side: lt_priming.py prime() (96-103) sets theta from the tier ladder (base THETA runs from 0.0 for Ally to 3.0 for Opponent, lines 19-21), adds a committed-opponent term and a money-captured term, and sums pressure over pro sources only (proset). Anti neighbours exert no competing threshold pressure. The recruit search (131-140) picks cheapest recruits per target rather than optimising a seed set, so submodularity is not invoked.
evidence.transfer: Thresholds here are not normalised to Borodin uniform [0,1] draws (base ladder 0.0 to 3.0 plus additive terms). Adding an anti-side threshold would be a model change for Paul to decide. Borodin monotonicity result is for the separated-threshold model and says nothing about this solver recruit lists, for which the paper gives no guarantee.

evidence.title: The Effect of Politicians' Personality on Their Media Visibility
evidence.claim: More visible MPs are less agreeable (beta -.116, p < .05) and more emotionally stable (neuroticism beta -.111, p < .05). The authors read this as media competition requiring psychological resilience (Discussion).
evidence.system_side: Default basis is behavioral (RECEPT_TRAITS defaults to behavioral, receptivity_layer.py:65). There seed_prob = clip(0.60 + .10 coop + .06 breadth_z + .04 visibility_z, 0.30, 0.90) and susc_trait = .40 coop + .30 Nn - .20 dil - .10 dom, where Nn is affective-content N with missing set to 0. The lexical fallback susc = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E and seed = 0.60 + .10A + .06O + .04E apply only when the basis is not behavioral.
evidence.transfer: On the default path the tension is real but indirect. Visible MPs in the paper have lower A and lower N. Lower cooperation and lower affective N both lower susc_trait, while visibility_z raises seed_prob. Inside seed_prob, the visibility term (+.04) and the cooperation term (+.10) can pull in opposite directions if visible members are less cooperative. This is not a measured US result: the paper's betas are small, self-reported and cross-national, and seed_prob is not an access or introduction probability (D-025). Check corr(visibility_z, coop_v2) and corr(visibility_z, affective N) on the roster; not yet run (DE-062).

evidence.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Voter Dynamics: The Role of Timing and Network Heterogeneity
evidence.claim: Vote share at a finite horizon depends on when each controller starts and on degree heterogeneity. At T=16 (dimensionless model time, unit-weight graphs) the degree of equilibrium l never exceeds 0.82 and high-degree nodes relax more slowly. An optimized start beats t_a=0 in all 30 rows of Table 2 (5 real networks, T in {16, 256}, budget ratio in {0.1, 1, 10}). Congress votes network, T=16, budget ratio 1: S_A 0.705 vs 0.500 (model output, not observed votes).
evidence.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where a and b are each a saturating money pull plus a party-weighted proximity term. It is a static, time-free share with no horizon, no start time and no relaxation lag.
evidence.transfer: Structural parallel only: both are ratios of competing pulls. Magnitudes do not transfer, since paper time is dimensionless, edges have unit weight and opinions are binary simple contagion. The paper shows that an equilibrium-share form omits timing, not that pflip is miscalibrated.

evidence.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Voter Dynamics: The Role of Timing and Network Heterogeneity
evidence.claim: Competitive influence is analysed in a non-progressive voter model with reversible opinions, where the opponent is a strategic controller choosing its own start time at a Nash equilibrium (Eq 9, Algorithm 2 p.8; Fig 8 p.19-20). The paper does not state that the second mover concentrates its budget in the final stage. Its text says the second mover starts later and can only buffer the first mover's gain (p.21). End-loaded budgets appear for the budget-advantaged controller when the degree exponent is below about 2.2 (Sec 4.3.4, p.21-22).
evidence.system_side: A two-colour first-to-reach independent cascade: a reached member keeps its colour for the rest of the run. Industry money enters only as non-strategic bystander activation, min(0.9, ind/400000). Nothing represents an opponent that responds in time.
evidence.transfer: This is a difference in model class, not evidence that the independent cascade choice is wrong. The original claims that cosponsorship is close to progressive with rare withdrawals, and that stance and votes are not, have no source in the paper or the code. Those claims are UNVERIFIED here and should not be relied on.

evidence.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Voter Dynamics: The Role of Timing and Network Heterogeneity
evidence.claim: In the individual-optimization runs with 20 percent of agents as partial zealots (Sec 4.3.3, N=100 per the Sec 4.3.2 reduction; N not restated in 4.3.3), normal agents receive more budget than zealots at every zealotry level q tested. At q=0.1 the maximum zealot allocation is under 20 and the normal-agent maximum is near 25 (allocation units as plotted in Fig 7). At medium and large q zealots get fewer resources and start later as degree rises.
evidence.system_side: PERS in moneyball_core.py gives Opponent 0.08, Highly Skeptical 0.15 and Champion 0.10, with middle tiers between 0.50 and 0.65. The F1 gate in optimize.py gives zero allocation to members whose overall tier is Skeptic, Highly Skeptical or Opponent.
evidence.transfer: The direction matches for resistant tiers (Opponent and Highly Skeptical). Champion is a committed pro tier, so its low multiplier reflects being already won, not zealot resistance, and it does not support the paper's result. The paper never sets zealot allocation to zero, so it does not support the hard zero gate on its own. Simulated agents only.

evidence.title: An Improved D* Lite-Based Dynamic Route Planning Algorithm for Ships in Arctic Waters
evidence.claim: Paper reports node updates of 18,468 vs 72,835 (freezing) and 16,864 vs 114,929 (melting) for its improved D* Lite against full global re-planning. Numbers are correct. The paper frames reuse of earlier search data as the motivation (Sec. 2.1) but does not say D* Lite family planners save work only by reuse.
evidence.system_side: scenario.py docstring (line 13) cites Ren et al. Multi-Objective Path-Based D* Lite for recompute only what the scenario touches. The code uses common random numbers (cascade, around :42-52) and recomputes spread and flip value for every category (:103-115). Isolation comes from CRN, not from reusing earlier search state.
evidence.transfer: Documentation point only. At 533 members and MC=40 a full recompute is cheap, so incremental reuse is not warranted. The Xu numbers say nothing about the cascade. The cited work is Ren et al., not Xu.

evidence.title: Emerging Late Adolescent Friendship Networks and Big Five Personality Traits: A Social Network Approach
evidence.claim: Effects of one person's own traits are small next to similarity effects. Extraversion predicts making more ties (ego .10), agreeableness predicts being chosen (alter .14), and openness has no ego or alter effect (.02, n.s.).
evidence.system_side: seed_prob uses only the member's own traits. The default behavioural basis is 0.60 + .10 cooperation_v2 + .06 breadth + .04 visibility; the non-default lexical basis is 0.60 + .10A + .06O + .04E, on the reasoning that agreeable, open and extraverted members take meetings. Nothing describes the match between a lobbyist or recruiter and the member.
evidence.transfer: Transfer is weak. The paper measures friendship nomination, not whether a contacted official acts. Within that limit, it gives no support to the openness term in the lexical basis. The agreeableness result concerns being approached, not acting once approached. The paper's main point, that pairwise similarity outweighs individual levels, shows a dyadic term is missing, but there is no legislative evidence for adding one, and the system's own persona-homophily test came out null.

evidence.title: Shadowing and shielding: Effective heuristics for continuous influence maximisation in the voting dynamics
evidence.claim: Steady-state opinions solve (L + Wa + Wb) x = wa for the voter model with zealots (Eq 1 rate equation on p.3; Eq 2 vote share on p.4). In the high-allocation limit (w much larger than d) the optimal allocation has no degree dependence (Eqs 7-8, pp.7-8).
evidence.system_side: flip_model.py pflip (lines 92-97): a = WM*pm*saturating CU term + WP*nA/mAt, with b mirroring it using industry money and anti-camp neighbours, returning a/(a+b). It is a one-shot ratio, not a steady-state solve. Neighbour camps nA and nB are fixed by stance; mAt and mBt are maxima over nodes (lines 132-143).
evidence.transfer: The functional form is analogous (a share-of-pull ratio), but the paper's neighbour states are endogenous while Melange fixes them from stance, so the paper's HMF results do not transfer. Read pflip only as a vote-share proxy, never as a vote or access probability (D-025). The analogy itself is an inference (DE-062).

evidence.title: Shadowing and shielding: Effective heuristics for continuous influence maximisation in the voting dynamics
evidence.claim: In the discrete regime optima are driven mainly by node degree (hub targeting). Shadowing and shielding matter mostly in the continuous regime, and shielding weakens as K grows (K = 256 in Fig 3c).
evidence.system_side: budget_frontier.py cascade(): progressive two-colour first-to-reach spread from A and B seeds over the P kernel with edge-keyed CRN draws. Bystander activation uses min(0.9, ind/BSCALE) (line 133). MAXSEEDS defaults to 60 (line 7).
evidence.transfer: IC is progressive (an activated node stays activated) and the voter model is reversible, so only the regime point transfers: seed-set optimisers will tend toward hubs, and opponent-aware placement matters more when allocation is continuous. One network and no noise in the paper. The lazy-greedy description of the frontier engine was not checked in this pass.

evidence.title: Mapping the Political Personality (PoliPers): An Integrative Framework for Assessing Ideal and Actual Personality Profiles in Politicians (version 0.1)
evidence.claim: Observer correlations in Table 5 (Trump n=104, Merkel n=107, Study 4, Apr 2021): Empathy with likeability r=.70 (Trump) and .76 (Merkel); Integrity with ideological proximity r=.46 (Trump) and .36 (Merkel); Intellect with proximity r=.48 (Trump). All proximity correlations are positive as printed. PoliPers tests no link from any facet to behavior under pressure.
evidence.system_side: persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) minus .40 z(agency), blended into susceptibility at PERSONA_W 0.30. The design presumes communal rhetoric marks susceptibility and assertive rhetoric marks resistance to pressure.
evidence.transfer: The correlations come from observers rating two foreign leaders on same-occasion ratings. They do not bear on how members of Congress respond to lobbying. Nothing here validates or refutes the persona signs, and the sign of the proximity association is unresolved (see verifier note).

evidence.title: Pinpointing the Powerful: Co-voting Network Centrality as a Measure of Political Influence (online appendix)
evidence.claim: Converting cueing networks into voting data loses network structure: simple networks are recovered best, moderate and complex networks less well, and betweenness recovery is only about 0.25 correlation.
evidence.system_side: build_P computes p(u to v) = w times cpf times sigma_v divided by (w times cpf times sigma_v + 6), a saturation kernel over cosponsorship-weighted adjacency with partisan factors cpf_diffusion and cpf_pressure. The kernel does not infer edges from roll-call co-voting, so the paper's conversion loss does not apply directly.
evidence.transfer: The paper's result concerns recovering node centralities from simulated voting records; it says nothing about cascade edge probabilities or the saturation constant 6. The analyst's claim that kernel edges come from cosponsorship weights was not checked, because load_network was not opened in this pass. Relevance is only as a caution against calibrating kernel edges from roll-call agreement. The evidence is simulation, not US data.

evidence.title: Cross-Industry Political Spending - Analysis Overview (memo)
evidence.claim: Bank CEOs give little directly to candidates; several, including Moynihan and Masrani, gave nothing across recent cycles. Bank money flows mainly through company PACs and the ABA (cyclical average $2,402,499, memo wording). Mutual-fund Super PAC spending (about $261M annual average to the four biggest Super PACs; industry PACs about $13M cumulative; memo figures, no source or window) is described as channeled by the industry. CU giving runs through ACU coordination, with $0 dark money to the four biggest Super PACs (memo wording).
evidence.system_side: flip_model.py line 39 builds cu0 from C[n]['cu'] and ind0 from banks plus finserv; the flip formula at lines 4-7 uses cu as the a-term and ind as the b-term. Only those two columns are read in this file. Whether the upstream cu and banks columns include trade-association or Super PAC money was not checked.
evidence.transfer: Structural caution only. The memo's dollar figures have no source, window, N or denominator, so they cannot calibrate WM, HALFF or the b-term. Before any engine change, Mentat's trade-association and Super PAC columns would need mapping to members.

evidence.title: Party Cues in the News: Democratic Elites, Republican Backlash and the Dynamics of Climate Skepticism
evidence.claim: A polarized cue (Democrats for, Republicans against) moves strong Republicans +0.09 points on the 0-1 scale (about 0.3 SD, p~0.002). It is numerically the largest cue effect, but the authors do not report it as significantly different from the single Democratic cue or opposing-GOP cue effects. A single Democratic cue moves them +0.06 (p~0.03). Supporting-GOP and consensus cues show no polarizing effect and no de-polarizing effect. Observationally, +100 articles a quarter with cues held fixed goes with -0.4 SD in Republican skepticism (Model 3, PCCTI, N=54; p~0.03).
evidence.system_side: Going public is three regimes. Retreat moves co-partisans +1 and out-partisans -1, matching the paper's polarized-cue backlash direction. Rally moves out-partisans +0.5 only when bpf is at least 0.30, which the paper's consensus null does not support. Regime probabilities p and q come from the D-R tier gap z in salience_issue_params, and the advisory actor party defaults to R.
evidence.transfer: Carries over only as a direction-of-effect prior. The paper studies mass partisans reacting to elite cues in national newspapers on climate; the engine moves legislators' stance tiers on credit-union issues. The rally result rests on one thin MTurk treatment, so it weakens but does not refute out-partisan rally movement. Treating z as endogenous to going public is the analyst's inference, not the paper's; the Granger results concern cue shares and skepticism, not the partisan stance gap.

evidence.title: Party Cues in the News: Democratic Elites, Republican Backlash and the Dynamics of Climate Skepticism
evidence.claim: Out-group (Democratic) elite cues move Republicans away from the cued position rather than toward it. Experiment: strong Republicans +0.06 toward skepticism (about 0.2 SD, p~0.03), with a party-ID interaction p~0.05. Time series: Democratic cues Granger-cause Republican skepticism (chi2 7.35, p=0.03, 2 lags); the reverse has p=0.86.
evidence.system_side: The Bakker cross-cue factor xf passes a cross-party pro-cue through sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), so a non-bridge out-party cue falls to about 0. The priming term is clamped at 0 and never goes negative; the code comment says backfire magnitude is not invented.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports that out-party cues do not persuade and reads as backlash, so a negative sign is consistent with it. But the +0.06 effect is measured on mass Republicans and one climate item, not on legislators reading cosponsorship signals, so it cannot set a backfire magnitude for the priming term. Keeping the zero clamp remains defensible.

evidence.title: Party Cues in the News: Democratic Elites, Republican Backlash and the Dynamics of Climate Skepticism
evidence.claim: Democratic cues move Republicans toward skepticism, away from the cued position, in both the experiment and the time series (backlash rather than attenuated persuasion). Republican cues have no aggregate effect (chi2 0.00, p=0.94) and only a weak effect on Republican skepticism (chi2 2.94, p~0.09). The authors say co-partisan sources dominate.
evidence.system_side: cpf_pressure gives an out-partisan source a 0.5x pull and a co-partisan source 1.7x; cpf_diffusion keeps a 0.4 cross-party floor. Both keep out-party influence positive and weaker, not negative.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports co-partisan sources dominating, which fits the 1.7 versus 0.5 ordering. It reports backlash, meaning movement away from the cued position, but estimates no multiplier relative to co-partisan influence, so it cannot show the out-partisan sign should be at or below zero rather than 0.5. Cosponsorship ties are observed behaviour rather than cues, so transfer is weak. The paper gives no support for the 1.7/0.5 ratio itself.

evidence.title: The persuasive effects of political microtargeting in the age of generative artificial intelligence
evidence.claim: Persuasion depends on the fit between message style and recipient openness, above and beyond the recipient's own openness: mismatch coefficient b = -0.07 (study 1a, n = 440) and -0.08 (study 1b, n = 804) per SD of |z(O_person) - z(O_ad)| on a 1-5 perceived-persuasion scale, b = -0.03 for ChatGPT-tailored ads (n = 804), with person and ad openness held as separate predictors.
evidence.system_side: The receptivity layer maps traits to person-level multipliers only: susc_trait = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E, susc_mult and edge_mult as affine gains of that one scalar, and on the lexical basis seed_prob = clip(0.60 + .10A + .06O + .04E, 0.30, 0.90). The default basis is behavioral (RECEPT_TRAITS defaults to behavioral), so lexical O does not enter seed_prob at all by default. No term varies with the content or framing of the ask; receptivity is message-invariant.
evidence.transfer: Holds only if trait-message fit operates for legislators receiving lobbying asks as it does for UK Prolific adults rating Facebook ads; the outcome is self-reported perceived persuasion, not a vote or cosponsorship; effects are small (simulated 2,490 per 100,000 at a midpoint cutoff). Any matching term would need a message-side trait score Melange does not compute, and would stay UNVERIFIED until tested against the prospective H1/H2 contract.

evidence.title: Pitch Perfect: Vocal Pitch and the Emotional Intensity of Congressional Speech
evidence.claim: Table 7, Model 7.1 gives 0.015 (SE 0.002) and Model 7.2 gives 0.012 (SE 0.002) for female speeches x female pitch on the share of male votes cast with female members. At +2 SD pitch (1.41 on the paper's scale), that share moves from 0.23 SD below to 0.53 SD above as female speeches go from 0 to 43 (Figure 3, p. 957). The authors say the data are observational and do not claim causation (p. 956-957). Vote timing is unknown (fn 31).
evidence.system_side: The cross-party cue weight is sqrt(bpf_u * bpf_v) (line 64). Searches of lt_priming.py found no intensity or pitch term in the cue weight or the pressure terms.
evidence.transfer: Weak and gender-specific: women's issues, 2009-2014, floor votes with no timestamps, not cosponsorship. The paper does not test a threshold mechanism, so it cannot set any engine constant.

evidence.title: Quantifying the potential persuasive returns to political microtargeting
evidence.claim: In the Study 2 calibration (n=3,990 respondents, 36 issues, 48 progressive video ads), the messages predicted most persuasive were often on obscure, low-information policies such as net neutrality. The authors offer this as one possible explanation for the Study 2 divergence, alongside a mixed pretest design and a nearly one-year gap before follow-up. They expect smaller effects in high-salience settings with countermessaging.
evidence.system_side: PERS is a fixed table keyed only on stance tier, with an inverted-U shape: Highly Persuadable 0.65, Opponent 0.08, and no-position default 0.45 via the PERS_NONE environment dial. It has no issue-salience or information term. Salience enters separately through fec/engine/salience_shock.py.
evidence.transfer: Weak. Tappin measures attitude change among public respondents after one video, while PERS models legislators under lobbying. The low-information point might carry over to members on low-visibility CU topics, but nothing here measures that.

evidence.title: Influence maximization in social networks: a survey of behaviour-aware methods
evidence.claim: Behaviour-aware IM adds user features (BV), relationship features (BE) and message features (AM) to the structural IM problem (Eq. 1). The survey reports no take-up rate, no effect size and no benchmark, and it classifies methods without comparing their accuracy. It warns that numeric encodings of attitude may not capture personality and that many users are silent.
evidence.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob(n) x SGATE[tier]). seed_prob = clip(0.60 + .10 coop + .06 breadth + .04 visibility, 0.30, 0.90) on the behavioural basis, and clip(0.60 + .10 A + .06 O + .04 E, 0.30, 0.90) on the lexical basis. The docstring cites Chen (UAI 2021) and this survey as its basis.
evidence.transfer: Supports only the framing that member attributes may enter seed activation. The survey does not discuss contingency-aware seeding, does not cover legislators, and does not justify the 0.60 baseline, the coefficients or the 0.30-0.90 clip, which remain design priors. Evidence route is H1: outcome_contract.py requires at least 150 members with cosponsorship deltas. The F5 count of 72 was not checked.

evidence.title: Influence maximization in social networks: a survey of behaviour-aware methods
evidence.claim: Trust-agnostic opinion-aware methods consider that all network relationships are positive (friend), whereas in reality networks may also include negative (foe) relationships. Trust-aware work uses signed graphs on the premise that opinion change depends on trust between users. The survey also warns that numeric friend-or-foe encodings may not capture attitude.
evidence.system_side: p(u to v) = x/(x+6) with x = w x cpf x edge_mult(v). cpf_diffusion (0.4 to 1.0) and cpf_pressure (1.7 or 0.5) change edge magnitude by party, never sign, so the kernel is trust-agnostic in the survey sense. The signed member-reference (LLM valence) layer is stated to be display-only; that was not checked.
evidence.transfer: A design taxonomy only, not evidence that signed edges improve prediction of Congressional cosponsorship. Adopting foe edges would need a second path showing that negative references predict lower future cosponsorship (DE-062). The survey's warning on numeric attitude encodings applies to the LLM valence scores. Signed edges would also change the two-physics architecture, so the owner decides.

evidence.title: Influence maximization in social networks: a survey of behaviour-aware methods
evidence.claim: Influence detection by simulation is the most expensive family, ranked simulation, then MIA, then RIS, then centrality (Sec. 2.2). Almost all methods model spreading with a conventional diffusion model, and changing that model may change accuracy significantly (Sec. 4). The survey gives no numbers for either point.
evidence.system_side: Competitive IC with common random numbers, MC=20 (budget_frontier.py:7; per_topic_coalition.py:6). Bystander anti-probability min(0.9, industry money / 400000) (per_topic_coalition.py:101). Kernel saturation constant 6 (build_P). The joint optimizer uses a Linear-Threshold flip model instead (optimize.py:4; flip_model.py:3), which this bearing omitted.
evidence.transfer: The survey gives no numbers, so it supports only a caution that outputs are model-conditional. The claim that RIS for two-colour competitive IC is not standard does not come from the survey and was not checked. The scenario count of 40 was not verified. The binding issue is diffusion-model validation, not speed.

evidence.title: The Gameability of Redistricting Criteria
evidence.claim: Population-based change and incumbent-based change can diverge sharply. In Minnesota, Plan 8 and Plan 9 have almost the same People Change (1.93 percent vs 1.90 percent), yet Incumbent-People Pair Change is 1.93 percent vs 13.90 percent, because one incumbent precinct was moved. The text says Plan 9 moves 0.03 percent more people than Plan 8, which Table 3 contradicts.
evidence.system_side: build_competitiveness.py takes House lean from Cook 2026 district PVI and Senate lean from the state PVI table. The ten-state REDISTRICTED set (AL CA FL LA MO NC OH TN TX UT) is flagged and never altered, and |PVI2026 minus PVI2025| >= 5 is flagged. Placement precedence is ballot-district override, then Cook incumbent match, then district number. No field records how much of a member's constituency was redrawn.
evidence.transfer: Holds where a member's seat was redrawn between the 2025 and 2026 maps. A constituency-turnover measure would be a sharper diagnostic than a state flag or PVI delta, but it needs block assignments for both maps and would only inform Paul's override review. c stays PVI-defined. Reciprocity is not validated.

evidence.title: Crypto-Oligarchy: The Cryptocurrency Lobby in American Politics
evidence.claim: Fairshake campaigned against Katie Porter in California's Senate primary and opposed Jamaal Bowman's re-election bid. The paper calls this influence 'decisive' and offers no counterfactual or estimate.
evidence.system_side: build_electoral_plays.py lines 30-34: for a genuine Opponent the primary route scores the same-party improvement gap and the general route scores the cross-party flip gap, and the value is the larger of the two. Verified.
evidence.transfer: Shows that federal primary-contest plays by an industry actor occurred in 2024. It is not evidence that such plays work, because outcomes are confounded and there is no comparison group. Do not use it to calibrate conversion.

evidence.title: Big Five Personality Predictions From Twitter Using Regression
evidence.claim: Pitches text-derived personality as directly usable for business targeting and mental-health uses (Sec 4), with no validation of whether traits predict any behaviour.
evidence.system_side: The project already ran this check and found against the paper's premise. The pre-registered nomological validation rated lexical Big Five as unfit for behavioural prediction (C reversed on participation; E reads as broadcast talkativeness), so receptivity susceptibility now defaults to a behavioural basis (.40 coop + .30 N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance). RECEPT_TRAITS=lexical is only a revert switch.
evidence.transfer: This is only a caution. The paper's implicit claim that a text-derived trait is action-ready is exactly what the system's single-look record refuted for legislators. Nothing in the paper should move the system back to a lexical basis.

evidence.title: The strategic advantages of micro-targeted campaigning: A proof of principle Bayesian Agent-Based Model
evidence.claim: Under Bayesian source-credibility updating, contacts restricted to receptive targets (credibility signal above 0.5) convert better than untargeted contacts. Contacting audiences who view the source unfavourably moves them away from the source's position.
evidence.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob x SGATE[tier]). SGATE falls from 1.00 for Highly Persuadable to 0.35 for Opponent, so the system already expects contacts with unreceptive targets to convert at lower rates. The model has no negative (backfire) outcome for a contact.
evidence.transfer: Directional agreement only. The paper's agents are voters, not legislators. Its unit is a source-credibility belief update, not a take-up decision about cosponsoring, and it estimates no take-up rates. The SGATE values remain unestimated design constants; this paper does not calibrate them.

evidence.title: Strategic identity signaling in heterogeneous networks
evidence.claim: The calibrated payoff model makes outgroup share of the audience the main driver of whether covert beats overt signaling, with cost a weaker driver, and covert messaging only reduces, not removes, outgroup dislikes.
evidence.system_side: The backfire probability b = min(0.35, 0.05 + 0.10 psi) depends only on policy uncertainty. The go-public advisory turns to 'quiet work' when the worst-case tail is large. Neither the backfire term nor the advisory uses the outgroup share of the audience being addressed.
evidence.transfer: The paper's audience is a tweet reader pool, not the Noble-Turner public-campaign setting. An outgroup-share term would need its own calibration on congressional data, and the paper's r_o = 0.5 cannot be ported as a parameter.

evidence.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Social Networks
evidence.claim: Independent cascade extended to two colours. Each edge gets its activation coin and an exponential delay fixed before the run. Lemma 1 builds a deterministic equivalent in which each edge outcome is fixed in advance and a node takes the colour of the path that reaches it. The paper's random tie-breaking applies only when several players select the same seed node, not to simultaneous arrivals.
evidence.system_side: Edge draws are keyed by iteration, u and v with no colour in the key, so one draw per edge serves whichever colour reaches it, and a coloured node is never recoloured. This matches the fixed-in-advance edge equivalence. The code drops the exponential delays and runs hop-synchronous spread. B is anti-tier members plus neutral bystanders drawn with probability min(0.9, industry dollars/400000); the code matches this.
evidence.transfer: Edge-level CRN and first-colour-wins carry over. Timing does not: unit hops replace the paper's continuous delays, so the paper's equivalence does not cover the system's timing. The bystander mapping (0.9 cap, 400000 scale) and the kernel constant 6 have no basis in the paper.

evidence.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Social Networks
evidence.claim: The paper avoids ties between simultaneous activation attempts by giving each attempt a continuous exponential delay. It randomizes only between players who select the same seed node. The rel claim that simultaneous arrivals are tie-broken at random is not in the text.
evidence.system_side: The cascade is hop-synchronous. The frontier is built A-first and children are appended in processing order, so by induction every A node in a layer is processed before any B node. A node reached in the same hop by both colours goes to A. Same-hop ties are therefore resolved deterministically in A's favour.
evidence.transfer: The departure from the paper's no-tie design is confirmed by reading the code. Its effect on CU reach is unmeasured. A rerun with B-first or randomized frontier order under the same draws would measure it. Remains UNVERIFIED under DE-062.

evidence.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Social Networks
evidence.claim: The best-response guarantee holds only for the last committer. Pure Nash equilibria need not exist and mixed ones do (lines 83-85). Theorem 2 bounds the price of competition at 2 on total activations, not on any one player's share. First-mover results cover only a duopoly on disjoint lines (Lemma 2, lines 149-153).
evidence.system_side: Scenarios hold industry fixed. Competitor money enters only as exogenous bystander probabilities (industry dollars over 400000, capped at 0.9) and as the comp leg of money_response, which was not opened. Industry never re-optimizes against CU's seeds. The scenario docstring limits the (1-1/e) claim to a follower facing a fixed opponent.
evidence.transfer: The fixed-opponent framing holds only if industry commits first and never reacts. FEC filings are public, so if industry reacts, CU becomes a first mover on a general graph, where the paper gives no algorithm or guarantee. The price-of-competition bound says nothing about CU's own share.

evidence.title: The Role of Emotional Stability in Twitter Conversations
evidence.claim: Neurotic users post and retweet more, and calm users reply slightly more (Fig. 5, no values in the text). Neurotic networks form longer chains (average path 1.551 vs 1.334; diameter 6 vs 5), and calm networks have more mutual ties.
evidence.system_side: The receptivity layer puts affective N into susceptibility with a +.30 weight, on the Byrne premise that N degrades decisions under pressure: susc = .40 coop + .30 N - .20 dil - .10 dom. This feeds susc_mult and edge_mult on the cascade. The brain records that no N susceptibility signal has been demonstrated.
evidence.transfer: Celli measures communication style and ego-network shape, not response to pressure or persuasion. The data are anonymous 2011 public Twitter users with tagger-inferred labels, not legislators. The result gives no support for N as a susceptibility multiplier. The only thing that transfers is a caution: if text-N tracks posting volume, a volume confound could enter N. The system residualizes on E and party but has no stated volume control. That control is untested here.

evidence.title: Complex Contagion Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
evidence.claim: K-complex model (Eq. 1): activation probability p0 when at least K neighbours are active and p1 much smaller otherwise. It is motivated by Centola and Macy 2007 and Centola 2010 but not validated on field adoption data in this paper; the paper cites succeeding studies as support.
evidence.system_side: lt_priming.py is a deterministic gap model. Its THETA ladder runs from 0.6 to 3.0 (lines 19-21), adjusted per member by net_lean/120 and a commitment term for Opponent cells. Pressure is the sum of P[u][v] times a cross-cue factor from pro neighbours. Money closes the rest, and recruits are cheaper pro neighbours (lines 96-145). Each target is solved alone and one hop deep.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports only the modelling option that adoption can be threshold-like. It gives no K or threshold values for legislators. Joint multi-target priming would be a new model needing owner authorisation and a holdout look.

evidence.title: Complex Contagion Influence Maximization: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
evidence.claim: IC and LT assume activation probability independent of how many neighbours are active, which keeps them submodular. Complex contagion breaks this (Sec. 3, lines 254-258 and footnote 2).
evidence.system_side: build_P (moneyball_core.py lines 555-562) sets each edge probability to x/(x+6), where x = w times cpf_diffusion times receiver edge_mult. None of these terms depends on how many in-neighbours are already active. cpf_diffusion (lines 543-545) uses a party term and a bridge factor bpf, which is network position, not a seniority or leadership term.
evidence.transfer: Context only. The paper gives no legislative estimate. Any count-dependent kernel would be a new model and must keep the two cpf physics separate.

evidence.title: Influence maximization in unknown social networks: Learning Policies for Effective Graph Sampling
evidence.claim: Every comparison uses a single-colour independent cascade with uniform p = 0.1, budget 10, and the mean of 100 simulations, with no variance or confidence intervals. Tables 2 and 4 report the best Geometric-DQN variant per test network or per test set.
evidence.system_side: The frontier runs a two-colour first-to-reach cascade over an edge-keyed splitmix common-random-number draw with default MC 20. Its kernel is p = x/(x+6), where x carries cpf_diffusion partisan damping and receiver susceptibility. Seeds come from lazy greedy over a priority queue on the fully known kernel P.
evidence.transfer: Gains measured under uniform p = 0.1 single-colour IC do not carry over to the system heterogeneous two-colour kernel. Any reuse needs a rerun on the system own P and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

evidence.title: A Congressional Twitter network dataset quantifying pairwise probability of influence
evidence.claim: Fink offers the directed pairwise probabilities as empirical transmission probabilities that can vary across edges. The paper argues that Monte Carlo SIR-type benchmarks usually assume one homogeneous, arbitrarily chosen rate.
evidence.system_side: For untied pairs, engagement (build_multilayer_network.py lines 117-122) and social (lines 158-166) probabilities enter as w = 6p/(1-p), capped by ENG_CAP and SOC_CAP, both default 2.0. In moneyball_core.py build_P returns x/(x+6) with x = w times physics times edge_mult, so it returns p when those factors are 1. For tied pairs, social multiplies the weight by (1 + 0.3 min(1, p/0.10)). Engagement on tied pairs goes through admit(), which drops them unless MEDIA_ADMIT is dominance, the default only in holistic runs.
evidence.transfer: The mapping holds only for untied pairs and only when physics and edge_mult equal 1. Fink rates are directed and normalized per source tweet, while the system symmetrizes them and reads them as per-campaign activation odds, which changes unit and meaning. The 2.0 cap gives p_max of 0.25. Fink covers one 2022 window and says the rates may not be stationary.

evidence.title: CampaignView, a database of policy platforms and biographical narratives for congressional candidates
evidence.claim: Platform text for 5,228 of 6,016 (86.9%) major-party ballot-eligible House primary candidates 2018-2022, with 43,465 hand-topic-coded platform points. Identifiers are FECCandID (not universal) and BioGuideID (incumbents only).
evidence.system_side: build_electoral_plays.py: the contest route primary term takes, per category, the Opponent's shortfall against the same-party average avgP, keeps only the negative parts, and divides the sum by the number of categories. So it is a mean-style proxy, not a plain sum. No challenger data enters.
evidence.transfer: House only, 2018-2022 cycles; the 14 topic codes are not CU categories. BioGuideID is incumbent-only and the paper advises against aggregating by either ID. Challenger coverage gaps (low fundraising, uncompetitive races) are where the proxy matters most. New analysis stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

evidence.title: Simulated redistricting plans for the analysis and evaluation of redistricting in the United States
evidence.claim: District partisanship is a function of the map. In Georgia the enacted 12th and 14th districts have 2020 presidential Democratic two-party shares above the range of 5,000 simulated plans (p.8, Fig. 2). Partisan metrics depend on the statewide elections available in each state, so cross-state comparisons are not valid (p.5, p.8).
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0 x exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0), where lean is one Cook PVI point oriented to the member's party. AL CA FL LA MO NC OH TN TX UT are FLAGGED as mid-decade redistricted, never altered. A separate flag fires when the 2025-to-2026 PVI shift is 5 or more points. Retirees take their 2025 seat PVI through ballot overrides. c carries no uncertainty term.
evidence.transfer: The ensembles cover 2020-cycle maps only. They do not include the 2025-26 mid-decade redraws that the system flags, and they describe counterfactual neutral maps, not the realized seat a member runs in. At most they could add a per-district map-sensitivity band or a cross-check of Cook lean against ndshare. Per the paper, ndshare is not comparable across states. Reciprocity and the c amplitude/scale stay unvalidated (D-104..D-108). This is not evidence for them.

evidence.title: An introduction to grf
evidence.claim: Best linear projection tests whether effects vary along a chosen covariate: financial.autonomy.index coefficient -0.0329 (SE 0.0128, p = 0.0099). Other terms: is.female p = 0.17, family cash transfer p = 0.066, is.unemployed p = 0.61. Heterogeneity can be hard to detect at moderate n (payday AUTOC t = 0.67, about 2,500 individuals; text says possibly underpowered).
evidence.system_side: PERS in moneyball_core.py: fixed table over stance tiers (Highly Persuadable 0.65, Persuadable 0.60, Ally 0.40, Champion 0.10, Opponent 0.08, no-position default 0.45 via PERS_NONE). Not estimated against observed stance movement after contact.
evidence.transfer: A BLP of contact effect on stance-tier ordinals needs logged contact and tier movement; the payday example suggests a sample of 533 members may be too small for tier-level heterogeneity. A null would not refute the table.

evidence.title: Q-Learning
evidence.claim: Q-learning needs each state-action pair sampled an infinite number of times (p.281). Lemma B.3 (p.284; proof p.290) says action-replay estimates of rewards and transitions converge with probability 1 as the level grows, under learning-rate sum conditions. This concerns estimating model quantities from unbounded samples, not learning a gate parameter. No finite-sample rate is given.
evidence.system_side: moneyball_core.py lines 626-630: SGATE is a literal hand-set take-up dict (Highly Persuadable 1.00 down to Opponent 0.35, default 0.85). gate() multiplies it by seed_prob with a floor of 0.15. These lines contain no update path from observed outcomes. No Chen 2021 reference appears in moneyball_core.py or optimize.py.
evidence.transfer: Learning take-up rates would need repeated observed contact-to-action outcomes per stance tier, which the system does not log. The paper's result is asymptotic and gives no sample size. The link is conceptual: Lemma B.3 concerns action-replay transition and reward estimates, not gate probabilities. Weak strength is right.

evidence.title: Maximizing the Spread of Influence through a Social Network (Theory of Computing extended version)
evidence.claim: LT is submodular when in-weights sum to at most 1 (Thm 4.6). The LT model draws each threshold uniformly on [0,1] (Sec 2). Thm 3.3, for the general threshold model, shows NP-hardness of approximation within n^(1-eps) for any eps > 0. Fixed-threshold models are only stated to admit no non-trivial approximation factor (p.117).
evidence.system_side: LT priming uses fixed per-tier resistance THETA from 0.6 to 3.0. Pressure is the sum over pro neighbours of P[u][v] times xf, with P the shared build_P kernel and no normalization to at most 1. Per target, recruits are taken by greedy sort on recruit_cost/add and money closes the residual. It maximizes no seed set and claims no guarantee.
evidence.transfer: Deterministic thresholds are the regime the paper excludes, so the greedy guarantee does not transfer. A future joint multi-target priming optimizer would inherit the n^(1-eps) hardness for general thresholds. Per-target cheapest tip remains a heuristic.

evidence.title: Maximizing the Spread of Influence through a Social Network (Theory of Computing extended version)
evidence.claim: Edge probabilities are set by rule, not estimated: LT weights from co-authorship multiplicity, IC uniform p of 1 or 10 percent, and weighted cascade p = 1/d_v with no multiplicity term (Sec 8.2, p.133). At p=1% each targeted node adds about three activations, so random seeds do relatively better (Sec 8.4, p.135). Estimating parameters from data is left open (Conclusions, p.138).
evidence.system_side: Shared kernel p = x/(x+6) with x = w times cpf times edge_mult. The saturation constant 6 is a literal design choice, not estimated. budget_frontier, per_topic_coalition and lt_priming each build their P through MBC.build_P. The scenario engine and others were not checked.
evidence.transfer: Seed rankings are sensitive to the activation level, so a sweep of the constant 6 (for example 3, 6, 12) should accompany any claim that frontier seed order is stable. This is not validation of the constant.

evidence.title: Small Campaign Donors
evidence.claim: Relative to safe Democratic seats, close races (mean Democratic winning margin between -10 and 10 percent over the last two elections) receive 0.11 pp more of a small donor's giving (48 percent of mean, not significant) and 0.18 pp more of a large donor's (75 percent of mean, significant at the 5 percent level). Sample is Democratic congressional candidates 2012-2020 with donor fixed effects.
evidence.system_side: moneyball_core.py:74-93 implements c = 1 + AMPLITUDE times exp(minus max(lean,0) over SCALE), with AMPLITUDE 1.0 and SCALE 5.0. The header calls these Paul's uncalibrated judgment constants and says the reciprocity they encode is not validated. c scales effective dollars on both money legs (cu and ind).
evidence.transfer: The paper measures where individual donors send money, not what a dollar buys from a legislator, so it neither supports nor refutes c. Quote the close-seat figures only as Democratic candidates only, UNSTRATIFIED by party.

evidence.title: Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?
evidence.claim: In the most common House specification (Column 1, 1978-1994, N = 3400, CCUS 0-100 score) an extra 60000 dollars of corporate PAC money (about 1 SD) changes the score by at most 2 points; 50000 dollars of labor PAC money changes it by 6; a change of party changes it by more than 30 points (40 with district FE). Member fixed effects eliminate the contribution effects, and IV reverses the sign on corporate money. Changes in donations to an individual legislator do not translate into changes in that legislator's roll-call votes.
evidence.system_side: shift_lean uses MAXSHIFT times r/(r+HALF) with r = c times amount over receipts. MAXSHIFT defaults to 18 with a code comment citing Ansolabehere for the cut from 40. On median receipts recomputed from congestion.json (1743281, n = 517), a 10k gift shifts lean by about 0.98, below DTHRESH 11.25. Defection needs roughly 1/6 of receipts before the pressure_mult and 1.10 LOSSFRAME factors, which can lower that fraction.
evidence.transfer: The paper estimates business-wide PAC money against a Chamber score at ordinary contribution sizes, pooled across the House. The defection channel fires only on scenario shocks near 1/6 of receipts, outside the paper's support. The member-FE null puts the within-member slope at zero, so any nonzero MAXSHIFT is owner judgment, not an estimate. The 2-vs-30 contrast is conditional on party and is not stratified; quote it with an UNSTRATIFIED label.

evidence.title: Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?
evidence.claim: Money is a small part of a reelection-minded legislator's calculation: party moves the score by more than 30 points against about 2 for money. The paper lists buying access as one of several group motives and does not test it. It cites 3 billion dollars of lobbying against 300 million of PAC contributions in 1997-98, and Langbein's estimate of about 10000 dollars per legislator hour. Its main thesis is consumption rather than access.
evidence.system_side: WM 0.35 and WP 0.65 at flip_model.py:21, with a comment that money buys access and effort more than votes, citing Ansolabehere, Hall and Wayman, and Kalla and Broockman. pflip = a/(a+b) with saturating money terms, each carrying a +1 smoothing term.
evidence.transfer: The paper supports money as the minority partner on votes, not on access. The access attribution rests on Kalla and Broockman, which is outside this paper. Peer proximity (cpf_pressure) is not party; the 30-point party effect is only the nearest analogue. With peer terms zero, pflip approaches 0 or 1 only at extreme money ratios because of the +1 smoothing.

evidence.title: Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?
evidence.claim: Closeness raises the quantity of money. In the gubernatorial panel (1976-2000, N = 326, state FE) the closeness coefficient on log per-capita spending is 2.93. In House races of 1992-2000, close seats (under 5 points) draw 60 percent of funds from individuals and 31 percent from PACs, while safe seats (30 points or more) draw 48 and 46 percent. Most of the gap in the individual share comes from gifts under 500 dollars.
evidence.system_side: c = 1 + exp(-max(lean,0)/5) scales effective dollars on both money legs; receipts stay in the denominators of pflip and shift_lean.
evidence.transfer: The paper shows the supply side only: more money, mostly from individuals, flows to close races. It says nothing about per-dollar influence. The PAC evidence is in shares, not dollar levels. Higher receipts in close seats shrink r and partly offset c. Reciprocity is not validated (D-104..D-108), and this paper does not validate it.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of Connected Legislators
evidence.claim: In the corrected column, between-party spillover is 0.8668 (SE 0.2136) and within-party 0.8346 (SE 0.0584); the gap is small relative to the SEs. The authors nonetheless conclude that cross-party ties matter more. House, 109th-113th.
evidence.system_side: cpf_diffusion damps every cross-party DR edge to 0.4 + 0.6*sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), which is 0.544 at the default bpf 0.24. Same-party and non-DR edges stay at 1.0.
evidence.transfer: The kernel models stance and activation diffusion, while the paper measures productivity spillovers, so cross-party damping may still be right for persuasion. Table 6 is not the only stratification: Table 5a and 5b heterogeneity, the Table 7 stage split and the Table 8 state-experience subsample (N = 1,775) also stratify or subset.

evidence.title: Difference-in-Differences with a Continuous Treatment
evidence.claim: A dose-response curve ACRT(d) is identified only under strong parallel trends; cross-dose comparisons otherwise carry selection bias ATT(l|h) minus ATT(l|l) (Thm 3.2). In the application the nonparametric ACRT(m) point estimates are negative for m above 0.41, covering 71 percent of treated hospitals, but the 95 percent uniform band covers zero everywhere, so only pointwise sign changes are reported. ATT_loc stays positive. A quadratic functional form is precise only if it is correctly specified.
evidence.system_side: flip_model.py:33-34 sets HALFF default 0.10. pflip (flip_model.py:92-96) uses (cm*cu+1)/((cm*cu+1)+HALFF*R). money_response.py:15-16 sets MAXSHIFT 18 and HALF 0.10. shift_lean (money_response.py:68-74) uses MAXSHIFT*(r/(r+HALF)) with r = amount/receipts. Code comments describe these as judgment dials calibrated against Ansolabehere and Fowler-Garro-Spenkuch, so 'literature priors' is a fair description. Neither file estimates a dose-response from panel data. The statement that the component's own open question asks about concavity was not checked.
evidence.transfer: A test would need a member panel: votes or stance before and after giving, an unfunded zero-dose comparison group, and dose as share of receipts. PAC dose is plausibly selected on expected response, so strong parallel trends is doubtful and any curve beyond ATT_loc would carry selection bias. This is a design template for a future test, not evidence on the current HALF or MAXSHIFT values. Any result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

evidence.title: Advancing the Empirical Research on Lobbying
evidence.claim: Lobbying spending was about 3.5 billion dollars in 2012, roughly five times the approximately 750 million a year in interest-group campaign contributions (pp.5-6). Kang (2012) finds expenditure effects on enactment are very small but the marginal policy return is about 140 percent (p.28), and the value of lobbying depends on timing and targets (p.28). Selection into lobbying (about 10 percent of firms) biases naive return estimates upward only if non-lobbying interests expect no return (p.17).
evidence.system_side: flip_model.py takes cu and banks plus finserv PAC money (cu0, ind0) through a saturating receipts-relative term. Lobbying spend does not enter the per-member legs: a case-insensitive grep of flip_model.py for lobby returns no hits.
evidence.transfer: Lobbying cannot enter a per-member leg directly, because LD-2 names no member and LDA is an identity source, not an edge or weight source (D-021). Pooled return figures must carry an UNSTRATIFIED label. Kang's 140 percent is a policy return in a structural model, not a dollar ROI.

evidence.title: Spillovers from regulating corporate campaign contributions
evidence.claim: Firm-cycles whose PAC reaches the limit are associated with 549,000 to 1.6M dollars more lobbying per cycle (abstract; Table 3 col 1; Table 5) and with about 110 dollars more CEO giving per candidate at the limit (Table 2). CEO giving is candidate money outside the PAC channel. Authors describe these as partial correlations.
evidence.system_side: The b leg of pflip counts competitor money as bank plus finserv PAC dollars per member (ind0), loaded from data/engine/congestion.json, with median imputation for unobserved members. Executive giving and competitor lobbying are not in ind0.
evidence.transfer: Hypothesis only: if competitor bank and finserv firms hit the cap as S&P 500 PAC firms do, ind0 undercounts competitor pressure on the members they max out. The paper does not test this. Does not license LDA dollars as a per-member weight (D-021).

evidence.title: The Bipartisan Path to Effective Lawmaking
evidence.claim: Within-member quadratic in the attracted share: House linear 1.828 and squared -1.844 peak at 0.496 (Model 3.1); Senate 1.666 and -1.626 peak at 0.512 (Model 3.4). Effectiveness falls on both sides of the peak. A one-SD decline from the mean costs about 22 percent of LES in the House and 16 percent in the Senate; a one-SD rise adds about 8 and 4 percent. Mean LES about 1.0.
evidence.system_side: flip_model.py:142 multiplies the target by (1+0.3*bpf). The inline comment attributes a passage bonus of +8-14 percent to Volden-Wiseman. No 8-14 percent figure appears in the paper text; its figures are 6-8 percent of LES per SD and the 22/16 and 8/4 percent shape numbers. The bonus is +7.2 percent at bpf 0.24 and +30 percent at bpf 1.0, rising monotonically with no peak.
evidence.transfer: A linear bonus approximates the paper only below a share of about 0.5, where most members sit (paper mean 0.29 House, 0.35 Senate). The paper outcome is LES on a member's own sponsored bills, not the value of flipping a vote, and its share is the attracted share, not bpf. Any change to the functional form would move ranks and is not proposed here.

evidence.title: The Bipartisan Path to Effective Lawmaking
evidence.claim: Cross-party cosponsorship is exchanged: members who offer cross-party support attract it back, within member 0.317 House (Model 4.2) and 0.547 Senate (Model 4.4), p<0.001. The paper tests member-level aggregates only, with no dyadic diffusion or join timing.
evidence.system_side: moneyball_core.py cpf_diffusion (line 543) returns 0.4 + 0.6*sqrt(bpf_n * bpf_u) for cross-party D/R pairs and 1.0 otherwise. The form is symmetric in the two members.
evidence.transfer: The paper cannot test the sqrt-product form or the 0.4 floor. Context only.
